intuition.text: Agreeing on a velocity gives the courier a goal, but it still needs an acceleration command. The actuator is where that agreement meets the courier's current motion and limits. A sensible output can be too small to keep an impossible promise, which is useful information for the earlier pipeline stages.
intuition.situation: A courier platform beside an inspection belt must match the belt's velocity before handing over a parcel. A marker on the belt makes the difference between matching speed and catching a particular position visible.

example.name: The inspection-belt courier
example.description: A courier and a belt marker start beside each other. The belt moves at the agreed {beltSpeed} units/s; the courier starts at {initialSpeed} units/s, with a speed capability of {maxSpeed} units/s and acceleration limit of {maxAcceleration} units/s². A response time of {responseTime} s sets how strongly it closes a velocity gap. The run advances by {timeStep} s for {duration} s. This is a velocity-channel actuator: public engine clipLength bounds the goal and matchVelocity produces the steering output. Study-local fixed-step integration applies it; target selection, constraint iteration and a full vehicle motor are outside this example.

step0.title: Read the agreed velocity channel
step0.text: The incoming agreement is the belt velocity, currently {agreed} units/s. Keep it distinct from both the courier's measured speed and the command the actuator will produce. The belt marker advances at this agreed velocity throughout the run.

step1.title: Bound the goal by the speed capability
step1.text: Use the engine's clipLength to restrict the velocity goal to the courier's speed capability. The feasible velocity is {feasible} units/s. This adapter keeps the original agreement visible, so capping it cannot silently turn an unmet goal into success.

step2.title: Produce steering acceleration
step2.text: Pass the feasible velocity and the current body to the engine's matchVelocity. It divides their velocity gap by the response time and clips the result to the acceleration limit. The actuator output is {acceleration} units/s², rather than a position update or an instantaneous velocity change.

step3.title: Let the movement harness apply the output
step3.text: The study-local harness advances velocity with the bounded acceleration, caps speed and then advances position with the updated velocity. At the selected moment the courier moves at {speed} units/s, leaving a velocity gap of {speedGap} units/s to the agreement. Equal velocities alone do not close the position gap of {positionGap} units.

pseudocode.ordinary:
agreedVelocity = velocityChannelFromPipeline

feasibleVelocity = engine.clipLength(agreedVelocity, maxSpeed)

acceleration = engine.matchVelocity(body, feasibleVelocity, responseTime)
// body.maxAcceleration bounds this output

velocity = engine.clipLength(velocity + acceleration * timeStep, maxSpeed)
position = position + velocity * timeStep

visual.textEquivalent: At {elapsed} s the courier is at {position} units and the parallel belt marker at {markerPosition}; agreed velocity is {agreed}, feasible velocity {feasible} and actual velocity {speed} units/s, while the actuator outputs {acceleration} units/s² and the position gap is {positionGap} units.

item0.explanation: calculateRealSteering subtracts the owner's linear velocity from the target's, scales the difference by the reciprocal of timeToTarget and limits it with the active maximum linear acceleration. intuition.text: A dock camera receives a compass heading, but its motor cannot simply adopt that heading. It must choose which way to turn, build angular speed and shed that speed before stopping. The awkward part is that a compass wraps: two headings on opposite sides of its written boundary can point almost the same way. Align makes the motor respond to their short angular separation.
intuition.situation: The dock operator wants the camera to copy the quay's inspection heading while its pedestal stays fixed. A smooth turn matters more than changing the displayed angle immediately.

example.name: Dock camera copying the quay heading
example.description: Camera starts at rest and turns through the short gap across the angle boundary towards the fixed Command heading. The slowing angle is {slowRadius}° and motor acceleration is limited to {maxAngularAcceleration}°/s². Each step lasts {timeStep} s; a small final correction finishes the turn only when both angular error and turning speed are within tolerance. Change the slowing angle to see braking begin earlier or later.

step0.title: Measure the short turn
step0.text: At this moment, command minus accumulated heading is {targetHeading} − {continuousHeading} = {rawError}°. Wrapping that difference gives {error}°, the signed short turn between the rays. Positive means clockwise in this drawing. A full-turn change in how a heading is written must not change the motor's instruction; an exact half-turn tie chooses the negative direction.

step1.title: Distinguish closeness from rest
step1.text: Accept a final snap only when the angular error is within {angleTolerance}° and angular speed is within {speedTolerance}°/s. Passing the command while still rotating is not a stop. The snap corrects the remaining small angle to the equivalent commanded heading and clears angular velocity; it is a separate settling rule, outside the normal acceleration update.

step2.title: Ask for an angular velocity
step2.text: Outside the {slowRadius}° slowing angle, ask for the {maxAngularSpeed}°/s limit in the error's direction. Inside it, scale that request by the remaining angular error; inside the angular tolerance, ask for no rotation so the motor brakes. The current request is {desiredAngularSpeed}°/s. These radii measure angles, so the drawing uses direction rays rather than a spatial slowing circle.

step3.title: Let the motor close the speed gap
step3.text: Actual angular velocity is {angularSpeed}°/s. Divide the gap to the desired velocity by responseTime, {responseTime} s, then cap acceleration at {maxAngularAcceleration}°/s² in either direction. The acceleration now used is {acceleration}°/s². A smaller desired speed can therefore coexist with continued rotation towards the command: the camera is braking, not instantly stopped.

step4.title: Turn through one fixed step
step4.text: If the settling test fails, add acceleration times {timeStep} s to angular velocity, cap the result at the angular speed limit, then turn using that updated velocity. Otherwise use the small settling snap. The next state has {nextAngularSpeed}°/s and accumulated heading {nextHeading}°. Camera stays on its pedestal; neither ray asks it to travel.

pseudocode.ordinary:
rawError = targetHeading - heading
error = wrapDegrees(rawError)  // half-open: negative half-turn to positive half-turn

if abs(error) <= angleTolerance and abs(angularVelocity) <= speedTolerance:
  equivalentCommand = targetHeading - (rawError - error)
  return { heading: equivalentCommand, angularVelocity: 0 }

desired = 0
if abs(error) > angleTolerance:
  desired = sign(error) * maxAngularSpeed
  desired *= min(1, abs(error) / slowRadius)

requested = (desired - angularVelocity) / responseTime
acceleration = clamp(requested, -maxAngularAcceleration, maxAngularAcceleration)

angularVelocity = clamp(angularVelocity + acceleration * timeStep,
                        -maxAngularSpeed, maxAngularSpeed)
heading = heading + angularVelocity * timeStep
return { heading, angularVelocity }

intuition.text: Imagine moving a character to a marked spot. Pointing toward it is easy; getting there without sailing past it takes a second decision: how fast should we still be going? Arrive reduces the desired speed as the remaining distance shrinks.
intuition.situation: A unit told to walk to a flag should stop on the flag, not run past it and turn back.

example.name: A character walking to a marked spot
example.description: One character starts at rest 100 units from a fixed target and moves along a straight line. Maximum speed is 16 units/s, maximum acceleration {maxAcceleration} units/s², the slowing radius {slowRadius} units and the response time 0.4 s. Each step is 0.1 s, and the final snap needs both distance and speed within 0.3 of zero. These are teaching values, separate from the catalog's scene defaults.

authored.by: Claude Code, the catalog's reading author

step0.title: Recognize an actual stop
step0.text: A character can pass close to the target while still moving quickly. Stop only when both remaining distance and speed are small. This example then places it exactly at the target with zero velocity.

step1.title: Choose a desired velocity
step1.text: sign(offset) chooses left or right. min(1, distance / slowRadius) keeps the requested speed at its maximum outside the slowing zone, then reduces it toward zero inside. This is the velocity we want; the actual velocity takes time to catch up.

step2.title: Limit how quickly velocity can change
step2.text: responseTime controls how quickly we try to close the velocity gap. It differs from dt, the time advanced by this update. clamp limits the resulting acceleration, so a large gap cannot cause an instant stop.

step3.title: Update velocity, then position
step3.text: Acceleration multiplied by dt changes velocity; the new velocity multiplied by dt changes position. The velocity clamp enforces maxSpeed. Using the updated velocity for position is the update order chosen for this example.

pseudocode.ordinary:
if abs(target - position) <= tolerance
   and abs(velocity) <= tolerance:
  return { position: target, velocity: 0 }

offset = target - position
desired = sign(offset) * maxSpeed
desired *= min(1, abs(offset) / slowRadius)

acceleration = clamp((desired - velocity) / responseTime,
                     -maxAcceleration, maxAcceleration)

velocity = clamp(velocity + acceleration * dt,
                 -maxSpeed, maxSpeed)
position = position + velocity * dt

intuition.text: A delivery trolley receives two instructions: go right to the delivery mark, and obey a marshal asking it to move left. Combining their strength answers a different question from deciding whose instruction wins. Equal opposing requests can leave a blend silent. Giving the marshal precedence produces a clear action, but handing control back to delivery can abruptly reverse the requested acceleration.
intuition.situation: The trolley should normally continue its delivery, yet a temporary marshal instruction may deserve control while it remains active. A weight expresses influence; a priority expresses authority. The example makes both policies visible on the same fading signal so that neither meaning has to be guessed from a single path.

example.name: The museum trolley and the fading marshal signal
example.description: Two lanes replay the same trolley starting at x = {startX}, with the marshal marker at {marshalX} and delivery at {targetX}. Engine seek produces each directional request at {maxAcceleration} units/s². The marshal's signal holds at full strength for {holdSeconds} s, then fades linearly over {fadeSeconds} s. The blend uses marshalWeight {marshalWeight} and goalWeight {goalWeight}; arbitration tries the capped marshal group before delivery and requires magnitude above epsilon {epsilon}. Both use {timeStep} s updates, a {maxSpeed} units/s speed cap and {steps} updates. The comparison changes only marshalWeight to {heavierWeight}.

step0.title: Give both policies the same instructions
step0.text: Sample the held-then-fading marshal signal from elapsed time. Engine seek points towards each marker; scale only the marshal request by that signal. At this moment the signal is {signal}, the marshal request {marshalRequest} units/s² and the delivery request {goalRequest} units/s². The signal envelope is study-local input, rather than a claim about a collision sensor. Each lane calculates seek from its own current trolley position.

step1.title: Combine influence with engine blend
step1.text: Multiply each request by its weight, sum the vectors and cap the result at maxAcceleration. These weights are multipliers, not probabilities and not a weighted mean. Opposite requests can erase each other before capping. The blended acceleration is currently {blendAcceleration} units/s²; equal authority is not inferred from a zero result.

step2.title: Select authority with engine firstActive
step2.text: Build each weighted group using engine blend so each already respects the acceleration cap, then pass marshal first and delivery second to engine firstActive. It returns the first group whose magnitude is strictly above epsilon; it returns zero if neither qualifies. The current winner is {winner}, producing {priorityAcceleration} units/s². A small change across epsilon can hand control to a request pointing the opposite way. Blending within groups and arbitrating between them is also a useful combination of the two rules.

step3.title: Apply acceleration without inventing an instant turn
step3.text: Update each lane's velocity with its chosen acceleration, cap speed and advance position using the updated velocity. The blended trolley is at {blendX}, moving at signed velocity {blendSpeed}; priority is at {priorityX}, moving at {prioritySpeed}. The chart measures acceleration, so a jump when the winner changes is a change of request. The trolley's velocity still takes time to reverse.

pseudocode.ordinary:
signal = clamp(1 - (elapsed - holdSeconds) / fadeSeconds, 0, 1)
marshal = engine.seek(trolley, marshalMarker) * signal
goal = engine.seek(trolley, deliveryMarker)

marshalTerm = { acceleration: marshal, weight: marshalWeight }
goalTerm = { acceleration: goal, weight: goalWeight }
blended = engine.blend([marshalTerm, goalTerm], maxAcceleration)

marshalGroup = engine.blend([marshalTerm], maxAcceleration)
goalGroup = engine.blend([goalTerm], maxAcceleration)
arbitrated = engine.firstActive([marshalGroup, goalGroup], epsilon)

for each policy's own trolley state:
  acceleration = policy == blend ? blended : arbitrated
  velocity = clipLength(velocity + acceleration * timeStep, maxSpeed)
  position = position + velocity * timeStep

visual.textEquivalent: At {elapsed} s the marshal signal is {signal}; the blended trolley is at x {blendX} with acceleration {blendAcceleration} units/s², while the priority trolley is at x {priorityX} with acceleration {priorityAcceleration} units/s² and selects {winner}.

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game-AI library with separate reusable combination behaviours. Its source gives a concrete design for combining influence with weights and authority with an ordered threshold test.
item0.explanation: BlendedSteering evaluates its children, accumulates each output multiplied by its weight and limits the resulting linear acceleration. PrioritySteering evaluates children in order and returns when the squared steering magnitude exceeds epsilon squared. Its documentation explicitly allows blended groups inside that priority list. The priority implementation returns the final child's small output if every child fails its threshold, which is a detail to check when adopting the library.

limits.item0: A blend can stall even though both children request movement. Raising the marshal weight removes this example's exact initial cancellation but changes the balance throughout the fade; a large multiplier does not give the marshal unconditional precedence.
limits.item1: Priority is decisive about authority, but a threshold crossing can abruptly change acceleration direction. With noisy signals it can repeatedly switch winners; this example uses a monotonic signal and therefore demonstrates a single handover rather than claiming to solve chatter.
limits.item2: A selected acceleration does not immediately reverse a moving trolley. Braking distance and the fixed update interval still matter under either combination rule.
limits.item3: The marshal envelope is a scripted instruction and the markers are directional targets. Neither run detects walls or tests the safety of the marshal's request. Arbitration can faithfully prioritise a poor request, just as blending can combine poor requests smoothly.

item0.why: Use Weighted blending when several compatible requests should all influence the trolley and the important design question is their relative strength.

item1.why: Use Priority steering when the marshal must take control whenever its group is active. It develops the ordered decision used in the lower lane.

item2.why: Use Epsilon threshold when tuning what counts as an active request, especially if a nearly silent marshal signal keeps taking control or noise makes winners switch.

item3.why: Use Equilibria in blending to diagnose the stationary upper-lane trolley before changing weights or introducing a fallback.

intuition.situation: A courier passes an oncoming porter in a loading lane. Only the courier adjusts its motion; the porter keeps walking. A small lateral offset supplies an unambiguous side on which to pass.

example.name: Courier and porter in the loading lane
example.description: The courier starts at ({courierStartX}, {courierStartY}) with velocity ({courierVelocityX}, {courierVelocityY}); the porter starts at ({porterStartX}, {porterStartY}) with velocity ({porterVelocityX}, {porterVelocityY}), in units and units/s. Their radii are {courierRadius} and {porterRadius}. The courier has maximum speed {maxSpeed} units/s and acceleration {maxAcceleration} units/s². The existing engine avoidance rule looks strictly less than {predictionHorizon} s ahead. This study advances {steps} fixed steps of {timeStep} s on an open plane, without the soldier scene’s field edges, braking or collision response.

step0.title: Put both motions on one relative clock
step0.text: Subtract courier from porter for both position r and velocity v. The time t = −(r · v) / (v · v) minimises the squared separation along their current straight paths. A negative time places that closest approach in the past. Equal velocities give no unique time. The local diagnostic draws both projected centres and reports t on every frame.

step1.title: Admit a future collision, or an existing overlap
step1.text: The engine first reacts to bodies already closer than their combined radii, using their current offset. Otherwise it accepts a neighbour only when t is positive, strictly inside {predictionHorizon} s, and the projected gap is smaller than the radii sum. With more neighbours, engine avoid retains the earliest accepted threat; this example has only the porter.

step2.title: Use the engine’s away acceleration
step2.text: The model calls scene-engine avoid for the actual steering. An accepted predicted offset is reversed, normalised and multiplied by {maxAcceleration}; no accepted threat means zero acceleration. A zero predicted offset remains zero after normalisation, which is the exact head-on failure exposed below.

step3.title: Advance the courier and the coasting porter
step3.text: The study’s local fixed-step update adds acceleration times {timeStep} to the courier velocity, clips speed to {maxSpeed}, then advances position with the updated velocity. The porter simply advances at its existing velocity. Recompute the prediction on the next frame: these are repeatedly revised forecasts, not a commitment to the first projected position.

pseudocode.ordinary:
r = porter.position - courier.position
v = porter.velocity - courier.velocity
t = undefined if dot(v, v) == 0 else -dot(r, v) / dot(v, v)
projectionTime = 0 if t is undefined else t
project both current velocities by projectionTime for the drawing

contact = courier.radius + porter.radius
if length(r) < contact: selectedAway = -r
else if t is defined and 0 < t < predictionHorizon
        and length(r + v * t) < contact: selectedAway = -(r + v * t)
else: selectedAway = null

acceleration = zero if selectedAway is null
               else normalise(selectedAway) * maxAcceleration
// The model obtains this result by calling sceneEngine.avoid.
// normalise(zero) stays zero; there is no head-on tie-break.

courier.velocity = clipLength(courier.velocity + acceleration * dt, maxSpeed)
courier.position += courier.velocity * dt
porter.position += porter.velocity * dt

item1.relevance: OpenSteer is a C++ steering library whose vehicle mixin includes avoidance between independently moving vehicles.
item1.explanation: The inspected code handles immediate close neighbours first, then projects both vehicles to their nearest-approach positions within a caller-supplied time window. It selects the earliest pair closer than twice the owner’s radius. Heading alignment distinguishes opposing, parallel and crossing traffic, choosing a lateral side vector. Crossing traffic steers only when the threat’s speed is no greater than the owner’s.

limits.item0: Changing only the porter’s lateral offset to {comparisonPorterY} makes the initial predicted centres coincide. Engine avoid then returns zero because there is no direction to normalise; the comparison exposes overlap before its current-offset response can resolve the encounter.
limits.item1: The forecast assumes constant velocities until the next recomputation. A turning or accelerating porter can invalidate it, and the fixed {predictionHorizon} s window is an engine constant rather than an adjustable study input.
limits.item2: One courier reacting to one coasting porter does not establish a rule for reciprocal crowds. Repeatedly choosing the earliest neighbour can change the chosen threat abruptly.
limits.item3: The courier can coast after the threat passes. This open-plane study supplies neither a destination nor a physics solver, and its collision rule does not detect walls.

item3.why: Time of closest approach isolates the dot-product calculation when the meaning of a positive, negative or undefined prediction needs closer study.

intuition.text: The Harbour survey trio needs to cross a quay abreast: Scanner watches one edge, Camera records the centre and Radio watches the other. Sending all of them to the survey gate would discard that organisation. Instead, move a shared pattern and give each robot its own moving place within it.
intuition.situation: Use coordination when individual movement must preserve a useful relationship between members. The shared task decides the pattern and its pace; each robot still needs a movement controller capable of keeping up.

example.name: The Harbour survey trio crosses the quay
example.description: Scanner, Camera and Radio start abreast around ({startX}, {startY}), with neighbouring slots {spacing} units apart. Their shared anchor heads for the survey gate at ({targetX}, {targetY}). Scanner and Radio can travel at {memberSpeed} units/s; Camera can travel at {cameraSpeed}. The anchor uses the engine's planning speed {anchorSpeed} units per planning step and lag limit {lagLimit} units. Each local integration step lasts {timeStep} s. The comparison changes only Camera's speed limit to {failureCameraSpeed} units/s.

step0.title: Give each robot a distinct place
step0.text: The public patternSlots function centres a line around the anchor. Public assignSlots maps the robots to left, centre and right roles using costs {preferredCost} for their own roles and {otherCost} for the others. Assignment happens once for this fixed crew; it is separate from steering to the chosen place.

step1.title: Move the shared reference
step1.text: Public advanceFormation steers the anchor towards the survey gate, moderates it towards the members' previous mean and caps how far it can lead that mean. Public slotPosition turns each relative offset into a world target. The anchor is a reference point, not another robot.

step2.title: Let each robot follow its own target
step2.text: Public arrive returns a bounded acceleration towards each moved slot, using slowing radius {slowRadius}, target radius {targetRadius} and response time {responseTime}. The study-local integrator updates velocity, caps it at that robot's speed limit, then moves position with the new velocity. It adds no separation or collision avoidance.

step3.title: Measure whether the relationship survives
step3.text: Measure Camera's distance from its centre slot and the mean distance of all members from their slots after each update. Distinct targets preserve identity, but do not guarantee that every robot can reach its target at the chosen pace. The lines joining bodies to rings make that difference visible.

pseudocode.ordinary:
slots = patternSlots('line', crew.length, spacing)
assignment = assignSlots(crew, ['left', 'centre', 'right'], costs)
formation = makeTwoLevelFormation(slots, assignment, start, anchorSpeed, lagLimit)

formation = advanceFormation(formation, previousMembers, surveyGate, timeStep)
targets = assignment.map(member => slotPosition(formation, member.slot))

for each robot, using the previous members:
  acceleration = arrive(robot, itsTarget, arrivalTuning)
  velocity = clipLength(robot.velocity + acceleration * timeStep, robot.maxSpeed)
  position = robot.position + velocity * timeStep

cameraError = distance(camera.position, cameraSlot)
meanError = mean(members.map(robot => distance(robot.position, itsSlot)))
remember(formation, members, cameraError, meanError)

intuition.text: A rover can see an obstacle perfectly and still have no useful decision. Point its matching whiskers at the two faces of a pointed wedge: each hit asks it to move away from one wall, towards the influence of the other. In this example the sideways requests erase each other, while their backward components erase the delivery request. The sensors keep reporting the same danger because the rover never changes its position.
intuition.situation: A delivery rover stops in front of a pointed display plinth. Logging more ray hits confirms that sensing works; it does not explain how the rover should choose a side. A persistent stall needs a decision that breaks the symmetry.

example.name: The delivery rover at the pointed plinth
example.description: The rover starts on the centre line at x = {startX}, facing a wedge whose nose is at x = {cornerX}. Its two walls extend {wallDepth} units right and {wallRise} units to either side. Delivery is further along the centre line at x = {targetX}. Matching whiskers have direction ratios ({rayForward}, ±{raySide}) and length {rayLength}. A wall hit requests its outward unit normal times {wallAcceleration} units/s². Engine seek supplies the delivery request; engine blend caps the sum at {maxAcceleration} units/s². The run takes {steps} updates of {timeStep} s, with speed capped at {maxSpeed} units/s. winnerRay is {winnerRay}, disabled; the comparison enables it so the upper ray wins simultaneous hits.

step0.title: Find actual finite-ray hits
step0.text: Normalise each direction ratio and extend it by rayLength from the current rover position. Intersect that finite segment with both finite wall segments and retain its nearest hit. The rings in the drawing are these calculated intersections, currently {upperHit} and {lowerHit}. Wall sensing is study-local because the public scene engine has no wall raycast helper.

step1.title: Turn each hit into an outward request
step1.text: A wall's perpendicular pointing out of the wedge supplies the correction direction. Normalise it, then multiply by wallAcceleration. The current requests are {upperCorrection} and {lowerCorrection}; engine seek adds the destination request {goal}. These fixed-strength normal requests are the teaching rule for this plinth, rather than a reproduction of a library's complete avoidance policy.

step2.title: Expose the conflict in the sum
step2.text: Pass the destination and all hit corrections to engine blend with equal weights. Its acceleration cap limits a large result but cannot restore a direction after cancellation. Here the net is {net}. The comparison changes only this admission rule: when both rays hit, keep the upper ray's correction and omit the lower one for that update. It chooses a side deterministically instead of waiting for rounding noise.

step3.title: Move, then cast again
step3.text: Add acceleration times timeStep to velocity, cap velocity at maxSpeed, then move using that updated velocity. Recompute the rays from the new position next update. With both hits admitted, the rover stays still and repeats the same calculation. The stall flag requires both hits, acceleration no greater than stallEpsilon and speed no greater than stallEpsilon; a small instantaneous sum while already moving would not count as this stall.

pseudocode.ordinary:
for side in [upper, lower]:
  end = position + normalise(rayForward, side * raySide) * rayLength
  hit[side] = nearest finite segment intersection(position, end, walls)

for each hit:
  correction[hit] = outwardUnitNormal(hit.wall) * wallAcceleration
goal = engine.seek(rover, delivery)

admitted = all hit corrections
if winnerRay and both rays hit: admitted = [upper correction]
terms = [goal, ...admitted].map(a => ({ acceleration: a, weight: 1 }))
acceleration = engine.blend(terms, maxAcceleration)

velocity = clipLength(velocity + acceleration * timeStep, maxSpeed)
position = position + velocity * timeStep
next update casts from this new position

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is an open-source Java game-AI library. Its raycast avoidance behaviour is a practical implementation of wall sensing and documents a corner trap in which alternating ray hits keep changing the chosen turn.
item0.explanation: The implementation updates a configurable set of rays, asks an injected collision detector for hits and selects the hit closest to the owner. It offsets that hit along its normal by the owner's radius plus a boundary margin, then steers towards the resulting point at maximum acceleration. Its class documentation proposes widening the ray fan or temporarily honouring a winning ray; those recovery policies are discussed there rather than implemented by this class.

limits.item0: The exact equilibrium is deliberately symmetric: the chosen wall slope, correction strength and destination request cancel at the starting pose. Other dimensions can produce sideways oscillation, contact or slow drift instead of a perfectly stationary rover. The failure is the unresolved conflict, not a promise that every corner produces a zero vector.
limits.item1: This short run demonstrates a local cancellation and the start of a detour. It does not supply a route planner, collision response or proof that the winning-ray run can reach delivery around the whole plinth.
limits.item2: The whiskers keep a fixed forward direction and use point segments. A turning body with width needs suitable sensor placement and swept collision checks; increasing ray length alone does not account for its footprint.
limits.item3: Always preferring the upper ray breaks this example's symmetry but can select a blocked side in another layout. A recovery policy needs a way to commit, detect lack of progress and reconsider its choice.

example.description: Nori starts at rest midway between the West and East beacons, each {beaconHalfSpan} units away along their line. Their seek requests have equal weight {beaconWeight}. The lower group uses engine wander with a fixed direction across that line, towards the bottom of the drawing, and fallback weight {fallbackWeight}. Requests must exceed epsilon {epsilon} units/s²; acceleration is capped at {maxAcceleration} units/s² and speed at {maxSpeed} units/s. Each update takes {timeStep} s. step0.title: Measure the combined beacon request
step0.text: Engine seek points at each beacon with full acceleration. Multiply both outputs by beaconWeight, then engine blend sums and clips them. The net request now has magnitude {primaryMagnitude} units/s². At the centre the opposing requests cancel; testing their individual magnitudes would miss that balance.

step1.title: Prepare an independent nudge
step1.text: Engine wander supplies a velocity-matching request from the fixed heading and wander circle. Engine blend applies fallbackWeight and clips the result, currently {fallbackMagnitude} units/s². This separate group contributes nothing while the beacon group has priority, even when its own request is stronger.

step2.title: Fall through only when the net is small
step2.text: Call engine firstActive with the beacon group first and the fallback second. Each must exceed epsilon strictly. The active group is {activeGroup}, supplying magnitude {selectedMagnitude} units/s². If both decline, acceleration is zero. No stalled flag or waiting period is involved.

step3.title: Move, then let the original group try again
step3.text: The local integrator clips the new velocity after acceleration × timeStep, then moves with that velocity. Recompute both groups from the new state. {primaryHandover} {returnReading} Moving away changes the beacon geometry, but a group can reclaim control only if its net request clears the chosen threshold.

visual.textEquivalent: Nori is {lineOffset} units from the line between West and East; {beaconReading}. The sideways fallback requests {fallbackMagnitude} units/s², and {activeGroup} controls this update.

item0.relevance: gdx-ai provides composable Java steering behaviours. Its blended and priority controllers can place a secondary request after a group whose ingredients might cancel.
item0.explanation: BlendedSteering accumulates weighted behaviour outputs and limits linear acceleration. PrioritySteering then evaluates behaviours in order, passing on when squared magnitude does not exceed epsilon squared. This makes a cancelling blend eligible to yield to a later behaviour. If all behaviours are small, the controller retains the last result, including a small nonzero one.

limits.item0: At comparison weight {weakFallbackWeight}, the first request has magnitude {comparisonInitialMagnitude} units/s² against epsilon {epsilon}: {comparisonStart}. Its largest offset is {comparisonMaxOffset} units. A fallback at or below epsilon cannot start Nori from this balance, even though the behaviour is present.
limits.item1: The chosen run reaches an offset of {maxOffset} units and uses fallback for {fallbackSteps} updates. {movementReading} {returnReading} Breaking the balance does not choose a beacon or find a route.
limits.item2: A small net result does not tell us whether Nori is trapped or already content. If both beacon goals are satisfied, the same fallback rule can move Nori away again. A completion condition belongs outside this magnitude test.
limits.item3: Zero acceleration does not stop a moving Nori in this integrator. An already moving body can coast even when both groups decline; only the initially resting case remains still without a request.

intuition.text: The dock operator points to the ferry's beacon instead of choosing a compass heading. The camera needs to translate that place into a direction from its own pedestal. After that translation, turning the motor is the same job as matching any other heading. The beacon may keep moving while the motor responds, so a correct target direction and an accurate actual facing are different things.
intuition.situation: A camera fixed to the quay should watch a ferry passing across the harbour. Its lens turns while its base stays still; the ferry's position, rather than its own facing, determines where the camera should look.

example.name: Dock camera tracking the ferry beacon
example.description: Beacon moves across the harbour with horizontal velocity {targetVelocityX} units/s for {travelDuration} s, then waits. Camera turns on a fixed pedestal with a motor speed limit of {maxAngularSpeed}°/s. Each step samples the beacon’s present position, derives a bearing and delegates the turn to Align. Change the motor limit or beacon velocity to see whether the lens can follow the changing bearing.

step0.title: Locate the beacon at this step
step0.text: At {seconds} s, sample Beacon’s position along its path, stopping its scripted travel after {travelDuration} s. Subtract Camera’s position to get a relative displacement; its direction is the dashed ray. The worked step shows both components, including why moving the pedestal requires recomputing the displacement.

step1.title: Convert the displacement into a heading
step1.text: atan2(dy, dx) uses both components to choose the quadrant, so a beacon to either side of the pedestal gets the appropriate bearing. The bearing now is {bearingText}. If both components vanish there is no direction to face: this example uses the current heading as a braking target, without inventing a bearing or drawing a sight ray.

step2.title: Delegate the turn to Align
step2.text: Align receives the derived heading, not the beacon's position. It wraps the difference to a short signed error, currently {error}°, and requests {desiredAngularSpeed}°/s against the actual {angularSpeed}°/s. Its {slowRadius}° slowing angle, {responseTime} s response time and {maxAngularAcceleration}°/s² acceleration cap yield {acceleration}°/s² now. It brakes inside the angular tolerance and snaps only when both angular error and angular speed are small.

step3.title: Apply the angular result and sample again
step3.text: Apply the returned heading {nextHeading}° and angular velocity {nextAngularSpeed}°/s for the next frame, keeping the camera at ({cameraX}, {cameraY}). Advance time by {timeStep} s and sample the beacon again. The motor acts on the bearing measured at the start of the step; Face adds no future-position prediction, so the beacon can move ahead of its gaze.

pseudocode.ordinary:
travel = min(seconds, travelDuration)
beacon = startPosition + targetVelocity * travel
direction = beacon - cameraPosition

if direction.x == 0 and direction.y == 0:
  targetHeading = heading  // no bearing: brake at current facing
else:
  targetHeading = degrees(atan2(direction.y, direction.x))

next = alignStep({ heading, angularVelocity }, targetHeading,
                 { slowRadius, maxAngularSpeed, maxAngularAcceleration,
                   responseTime, angleTolerance, speedTolerance, timeStep })

heading = next.heading
angularVelocity = next.angularVelocity
seconds = seconds + timeStep
// cameraPosition stays fixed; sample the beacon again next step

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game AI toolkit. Its Face behaviour adapts a positional target for the toolkit's reusable orientation controller.
item0.explanation: Face extends ReachOrientation. It subtracts the owner's position from the target position, rejects a direction near zero using the active limiter’s threshold, and asks the owner's vectorToAngle method for an orientation. It then calls reachOrientation with that angle. The owner's conversion determines the angle convention; Face itself adds the position-to-orientation adaptation and the zero-direction guard. Its guard returns zero steering.

limits.item1: Coincident camera and beacon positions do not define a bearing. This model brakes towards its current facing in that case; it can still rotate while shedding angular velocity. A game needs an explicit policy for that missing direction.
limits.item2: Face looks at the present position. It does not lead the ferry for a future photograph or projectile impact, and moving the pedestal requires recomputing the relative displacement. intuition.text: Mira's escort positions behave like marks painted on a board she carries. Turning her rotates the whole board, even while her feet stay still. A guard far from her has farther to travel for the same change of heading. Cheap target geometry can therefore demand expensive movement.
intuition.situation: A ceremonial escort can keep a recognisable shape in an open court if its leader turns gently. Before using the same arrangement for a quick pivot, check the movement demanded of the guards.

example.name: Mira's Lantern Court pivot
example.description: Mira halts in Lantern Court with an escort slot behind each shoulder. Each offset uses {spacing} units along both of her local axes, and her scripted turn lasts {turnDuration} seconds. Rings show destinations; the chart checks the speed needed to reach successive samples against a {speedLimit} units/s guard budget. The reference turn lasts {fastTurnDuration} seconds. The full scene separately uses Arrive to move guards towards these targets; this study isolates the fixed-slot geometry.

step0.title: Keep offsets in Mira's coordinates
step0.text: The engine makes a wedge for {members} members, then measures it from its leading slot. Mira occupies that origin, with escort offsets spaced {spacing} units along her local axes. Cache these offsets: a turn changes their world positions, not the pattern.

step1.title: Let the leader determine the frame
step1.text: The study-local schedule changes Mira's heading towards {turnDegrees} degrees over {turnDuration} seconds. The engine's advanceFormation copies her position and heading into the fixed formation without moderation. Her current heading is {angle} degrees.

step2.title: Rotate, then translate each offset
step2.text: slotPosition rotates each offset into Mira's forward and sideways directions, then adds her position. The escort targets stay behind her and {orbitRadius} units away throughout the pivot; the worked step shows the coordinate arithmetic.

step3.title: Check the movement the targets demand
step3.text: The local measurement compares each target with its preceding sample. The largest displacement is {displacement} units over {timeStep} seconds, requiring at least {requiredSpeed} units/s to reach the selected target. The budget is {speedLimit} units/s: {speedStatus}. An excessive request is reported without slowing Mira or clipping the destinations.

pseudocode.ordinary:
centred = patternSlots("wedge", members, spacing)
// Measure every offset from the leader at the wedge's tip.
offsets = centred.map(slot => slot - centred[0])
formation = fixedFormation(offsets, leader = Mira)

progress = clamp((step - turnStart) / turnSteps, 0, 1)
angle = turnDegrees * pi / 180 * progress
Mira.heading = (cosine(angle), sine(angle))
formation = advanceFormation(formation, [Mira], null, timeStep)

targets = offsets.map((offset, index) =>
  slotPosition(formation, index))

// Exclude Mira's own slot; the first sample has no displacement.
displacements = escortTargets - previousEscortTargets
requiredSpeed = max(length(displacement) / timeStep)
report(requiredSpeed, requiredSpeed > speedLimit)

intuition.text: Pip is a survey rover beside a hot test beacon. An escape instruction tells its motor which way to accelerate; it does not teleport Pip away or erase motion already heading inwards. Watch the velocity arrow as well as the outward push.
intuition.situation: Use this response when Pip should open a gap from a known point. This study runs the scene engine’s Flee: its push fades with distance, so the example also shows the boundary between asking for escape and deciding how motion should stop.

example.name: Pip leaves the test beacon
example.description: Pip starts at {start} on an open line, with the beacon fixed at {threat} and initial velocity {initialVelocity} units/s. Its motor allows {maxAcceleration} units/s² and {maxSpeed} units/s. Updates are {timeStep} s apart over a {duration} s window. The scene engine fixes its flee radius at {engineRadius} units; that is an engine choice, not a universal safe distance.

step0.title: Find the direction away
step0.text: Subtract the beacon’s position from Pip’s: the signed displacement is {offset} and its magnitude is {distance} units. Normalising this displacement chooses away. At exact coincidence the displacement supplies no direction, so this engine returns no push.

step1.title: Ask the engine for its fading push
step1.text: Call scene-engine flee on the current body and beacon. Inside its fixed {engineRadius}-unit radius it scales the away direction by maxAcceleration times the remaining fraction of the radius. Here the fade is {fade} and the signed acceleration is {acceleration} units/s². At or beyond the radius the output is zero. This differs from a constant maximum-acceleration Flee.

step2.title: Let the motor change velocity
step2.text: Multiply the acceleration by {timeStep} s and add it to velocity, then enforce the {maxSpeed} units/s speed limit. Acceleration changes motion over time: an inward-moving Pip can continue towards the beacon while the outward push brakes it.

step3.title: Move with the new velocity
step3.text: Advance position using that updated velocity. The next position is {nextPosition} units. This study-local open-line motor keeps existing velocity when Flee becomes silent; it adds neither a stop at the circle nor the full scene’s other steering rules.

pseudocode.ordinary:
offset = position - threat
distance = abs(offset)
body = bodyAt(position, velocity, maxSpeed, maxAcceleration)

acceleration = sceneEngine.flee(body, point(threat))
// engine: normalise(offset) * maxAcceleration * max(0, 1 - distance / engineRadius)
// normalise(0) is 0

velocity = clamp(velocity + acceleration * timeStep,
                 -maxSpeed, maxSpeed)

position = position + velocity * timeStep

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game-AI library with steering behaviours over either planar or spatial vectors. Its Flee class is a small reusable implementation of repulsion from a target position.
item0.explanation: Flee extends Seek and reverses the position subtraction. It normalises the resulting vector, scales it to the configured maximum linear acceleration and sets angular acceleration to zero. The class returns a steering output for game code to apply; this method contains no distance fade or stopping rule.

limits.item0: With Pip exactly on the beacon and initially still, the away vector is zero. The comparison changes only starting position and leaves Pip stuck; choosing an escape direction needs another rule.
limits.item1: An outward acceleration does not immediately reverse an inward velocity. Pip can move closer before the motor has removed that approach speed.
limits.item2: Leaving the response circle means the push is silent, not that Pip has stopped or reached a safe destination. This motor coasts; a complete game must decide what follows the escape instruction.
limits.item3: The example has an open line and a fixed beacon. The rule reads neither obstacles nor a moving threat’s future position, so it cannot select a route around a barrier or anticipate an interception.

intuition.text: Mara can make room for Ivo without knowing where Noor plans to stand. Each walker adjusts against the people currently nearby, and their repeated adjustments make the crowd look organised. The useful result is a moving group with room between its members; agreeing on velocity alone would also describe a moving pile.
intuition.situation: Mara, Ivo and Noor are crossing Reed Field abreast. Ivo starts faster. They need to travel east together without collapsing onto the same position, and there is no leader assigning places.

example.name: The Reed Field crossing
example.description: Mara starts above Ivo, with Noor below him. Each reads a circular neighbourhood, arriving towards its centre and matching its mean velocity while separation can leave room between them. Separation currently has weight {separationWeight}; a separate eastward drive has weight {cruiseWeight}. Change either control to expose crowding or a fading crossing. The model calls the scene engine for the steering and blend; neighbourhood selection and the simultaneous fixed-step update are study-local, independent of the scene's group-wide neighbour policy and cruising rule.

step0.title: Read neighbours from one snapshot
step0.text: Mara sees {neighbours} other walkers strictly within {neighbourRadius} units. Exclude Mara from their mean position and velocity. Every walker reads the same old frame, so updating Mara first cannot move Ivo's inputs; an empty neighbourhood supplies neither cohesion nor alignment.

step1.title: Ask for room and for company
step1.text: The engine's linear separation fades to nothing at its threshold and caps the combined push. Cohesion calls engine arrive at the neighbour centre, using a point target and a slowing radius; correcting towards that desired velocity also brakes existing motion. Mara's weighted separation and cohesion have magnitudes {separationMagnitude} and {cohesionMagnitude} units/s²; the worked step shows their directions.

step2.title: Agree on motion and supply a crossing direction
step2.text: Engine matchVelocity tries to close the gap to the neighbours' mean velocity over {responseTime} s. The separate crossing drive uses the same engine function with an eastward target velocity of {cruiseSpeed} units/s and weight {cruiseWeight}. The drive supplies travel; alignment cannot invent it when everyone is still.

step3.title: Blend the requests, then cap the sum
step3.text: Multiply each engine output by its weight, add the vectors and call engine blend to cap the sum at {maxAcceleration} units/s². The weights are strengths, not percentages, and each component already obeys its own acceleration cap. The requested sum has magnitude {requestedMagnitude}; the capped result has magnitude {accelerationMagnitude} units/s². Opposite requests can cancel before the cap is reached.

step4.title: Move everyone together
step4.text: Add acceleration times {timeStep} seconds to velocity, limit speed, then move with the updated velocity and publish all new bodies together. Mara's speed is {speed} units/s. The closest pair is {gap} units apart, while the chart's RMS disagreement with the group mean is {spread} units/s: spacing and agreement about motion answer different questions.

pseudocode.ordinary:
old = snapshot(walkers)
for each body in old:
  local = old within neighbourRadius of body, including body
  neighbours = local excluding body
  centre = mean(neighbours.positions) when nonempty
  meanVelocity = mean(neighbours.velocities) when nonempty

  separation = engine.separate(body, indexInLocal, local,
    threshold = separationThreshold, falloff = linear)
  cohesion = zero when neighbours is empty, otherwise
    engine.arrive(body, centre, slowRadius, targetRadius = 0, responseTime)

  alignment = zero when neighbours is empty, otherwise
    engine.matchVelocity(body, meanVelocity, responseTime)
  cruise = engine.matchVelocity(body, (cruiseSpeed, 0), responseTime)

  acceleration = engine.blend([
    (separationWeight, separation), (cohesionWeight, cohesion),
    (alignmentWeight, alignment), (cruiseWeight, cruise)
  ], maxAcceleration)

  nextVelocity = clipLength(body.velocity + acceleration * timeStep, maxSpeed)
  next[body] = body with velocity = nextVelocity,
    position = body.position + nextVelocity * timeStep
walkers = next

limits.item0: The crossing-drive weight is {cruiseWeight}. A blending equilibrium can be useful spacing or an unwanted standstill: outward separation can balance inward cohesion while velocity matching is already satisfied. Remove the drive from an initially still, symmetric group and active rules can leave it stationary. A small resultant alone cannot distinguish success from a deadlock; a priority or fallback policy must make that decision.
limits.item1: Separation currently has weight {separationWeight}, and the smallest sampled gap in this run is {minimumGap} units against a contact distance of {diameter} units. Lowering separation can leave velocity agreement working while the walkers pile up; reading the velocity-spread chart alone would miss that failure.
limits.item2: Separation reacts to current distances. It does not reserve space or predict a collision: fast walkers can pass through each other between samples, even with the separation weight enabled.
limits.item3: With no neighbours, a walker has no centre or mean velocity to follow. The model silences those terms and retains the crossing drive; a disconnected walker receives no regrouping instruction.
limits.item4: A local crowd controller contains no knowledge of paths, walls or a formation's assigned places. The public implementations add perception, arbitration and world handling explicitly; these are additional design choices, not consequences of choosing flock weights.

item0.why: Read Separation when the crossing already has a useful direction and the remaining problem is leaving room between neighbours.

item1.why: Read Velocity matching when walkers already occupy suitable positions but disagree about their motion; it will not create spacing or a travel goal.

item2.why: Use Arrive for the speed correction behind cohesion, or when the group must slow down at a marked destination rather than keep crossing the field.

item3.why: Reach for Equilibrium fallback when a near-zero blend leaves an unfinished task motionless and another behaviour should supply movement.

item4.why: Choose Fixed formations when named walkers must keep assigned places instead of accepting whichever spacing emerges.

intuition.text: A formation manager should be able to ask for places without knowing how a wedge is constructed. The pattern is a geometry strategy: it accepts a roster size, supplies indexed offsets and reports the centre of the places actually in use. That last answer matters when a roster has holes. A shape centred for the complete roster need not be centred for the members who remain.
intuition.situation: At the harbour rendezvous the lookout leaves to inspect the beacon. Port and starboard retain their wing slots while the escort turns. Their manager must distinguish the full wedge's centre from the centre of the occupied slots.

example.name: The harbour lookout leaves its slot
example.description: The lookout leaves a {capacity}-place wedge with spacing {spacing}, leaving port and starboard in their original wing slots. Drift correction is {correctionState}: {correctionReading}. The heading then turns by {turnDegrees} degrees while the escorts follow the chosen targets.

step0.title: Configure a contract with a capacity
step0.text: Configure the local adapter for a {capacity}-place {pattern} with spacing {spacing}. It accepts a positive whole roster no larger than {capacity}; the current answer for {activeCount} members is {supportAnswer}. Its slotOffset method checks the index and returns an offset from the engine's patternSlots. The capacity is a choice for this escort, not an engine limit. The engine has no public pattern object with support and occupied-drift queries, so those queries belong to the study adapter. Equal-cost engine assignment establishes the original identities before anyone leaves.

step1.title: Ask about the places still occupied
step1.text: When the lookout departs at {releaseSeconds} s, remove its assignment while keeping the wing indices. Compute drift from the occupied offsets, rather than robot positions or the whole stored table. Its magnitude is currently {driftLength} units. The engine centred the complete pattern; a subset can still have a displaced centre. Changing the motors or delaying a robot does not change this geometric answer.

step2.title: Subtract locally, then transform
step2.text: Drift correction is {correctionState}: multiply the occupied-slot drift by {driftCorrection} before subtracting it from each local offset. Turn the heading by {turnDegrees} degrees between {turnStartSeconds} and {turnEndSeconds} s. The engine's slotPosition rotates and translates the chosen offsets; the target mean is {targetGap} units from the anchor. The muted dots keep the complete pattern offsets unchanged, so they show the geometric bias that correction removes.

step3.title: Let the members approach the answers
step3.text: The engine's arrive accelerates each escort towards its assigned target, using slowing radius {slowRadius} and response time {responseTime}. Speed is limited to {memberSpeed} units/s and acceleration to {memberAcceleration} units/s². Local integration updates velocity before position over {timeStep} s. The actual mean is {centreGap} units from the anchor: changing target geometry does not move the robots instantly. The chart separates occupied drift, target-centre error and actual-centre error. The comparison changes only drift subtraction.

pseudocode.ordinary:
pattern = localAdapter(patternSlots(patternName, capacity, spacing))
if not pattern.supportsSlots(roster.length): reject roster
# supportsSlots accepts positive integers no greater than capacity.
assignment = assignSlots(roster, equalRoles, equalCosts)
# slotOffset rejects indices outside the configured slot table.

if step >= releaseStep: remove lookout and its assignment
occupied = assignment.map(entry => entry.slot)
if not pattern.supportsSlots(occupied.length): reject roster
drift = pattern.driftOffset(occupied)
# driftOffset averages pattern.slotOffset(i) for occupied indices only.

angle = turnDegrees * radiansPerDegree * turnProgress(step)
heading = (engine.cosine(angle), engine.sine(angle))
for each stored slot:
  correctedOffset = pattern.slotOffset(slot) - driftCorrection * drift
formation = fixedAnchorAndHeading(correctedOffsets, assignment)
for each occupied slot:
  target[slot] = slotPosition(formation, slot)

for each member:
  a = arrive(member, target[assignedSlot(member)],
             slowRadius, targetRadius, responseTime)
  velocity = clipLength(member.velocity + a * dt, memberSpeed)
  position = member.position + velocity * dt
# Keep the anchor fixed; update its scripted heading on the next step.

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java library of game AI algorithms. Its FormationPattern interface lets a formation manager use different geometries through the same slot-query contract.
item0.explanation: The interface exposes slot-count configuration, indexed slot locations and a support query. DefensiveCircleFormationPattern distributes slots around a circle, derives its radius from member radius and slot count, and faces members outwards; its support method accepts every count. Drift is owned separately: FormationMotionModerator averages occupied pattern locations, and Formation consults the optional moderator while updating member targets. The separation of geometry, assignment and moderation is explicit in the code.

limits.item0: After the lookout leaves, omitting drift subtraction displaces the target centre by {departureDriftLength} units. Better acceleration can reduce tracking delay but cannot centre a target set whose geometry is displaced. The comparison isolates that error by changing only driftCorrection.
limits.item1: A successful count query says that this adapter can supply indexed places. It does not prove that the quay has room, that robot bodies clear each other, or that a route to each place exists.
limits.item2: Retaining the original slot table is deliberate here. Regenerating a smaller pattern, reassigning members or moving the anchor to preserve existing world targets are other roster policies; they produce different movement after departure.
limits.item3: The drift is measured in the pattern's local frame. Subtracting it as an unrotated world displacement gives the wrong answer during the turn. This adapter handles positional drift only; it supplies no independent slot-facing or angular-drift contract.

item0.why: Use scalable formations when the geometry should expand, contract or regenerate as the roster size changes, rather than retaining holes in the configured table.

item1.why: Read formation manager when deciding who owns assignments, departure handling and updates; the pattern supplies geometric answers to that manager.

item2.why: Read drift offset when the main difficulty is reconciling the occupied slots' centre with the anchor, especially after the roster changes.

item3.why: Use two-level formation steering when the anchor must travel and its progress must respond to where the real members have reached. Geometric drift alone supplies no such feedback.

intuition.text: Lantern squad is told to reach a beacon together. Sending everyone to the same point loses the squad’s shape; assigning moving posts lets each member travel towards a different destination while sharing a group plan. The plan must still respect the people following it: a moving marker can ask more of the medic than the medic can maintain.
intuition.situation: North and south escorts flank a slower medic on open ground. The squad needs a recognisable line while travelling, then a near and slow arrival at the beacon. Its commander chooses an acceptable slot error rather than assuming the line will stay exact.

example.name: Lantern squad’s beacon march
example.description: North and South escort the medic in fixed posts on a line abreast. The selected anchor pace is {anchorSpeed} units per planning step: {shapeOutcome}. Followers read the old slots and move together before the anchor reads their new mean. The comparison changes only the anchor pace to {comparisonPace}.

step0.title: Give each member a different moving post
step0.text: Engine patternSlots centres a line with spacing {spacing}. The escorts keep the outer assignments and the medic the middle assignment throughout the march. The rings share the anchor’s forward position and retain those side-to-side offsets.

step1.title: Ask how fast each follower should go
step1.text: Every member reads its own old slot. Engine arrive asks for no speed inside stop distance {stopDistance}, full personal speed outside slow radius {slowRadius}, and a linear ramp between. It closes that velocity gap over response time {responseTime}, with acceleration magnitude capped at {accelerationLimit}.

step2.title: Move followers from the same snapshot
step2.text: The study-local update adds acceleration × {timeStep} to velocity, caps it at each member’s speed limit, then adds new velocity × {timeStep} to position. Everyone reads the same old snapshot. The medic now moves at {medicSpeedNow} units/s and the escorts at {escortSpeedNow} units/s.

step3.title: Move the plan while keeping contact with the squad
step3.text: Engine advanceFormation reads the updated member mean. Anchor pace {anchorSpeed} is distance per {planningSeconds} s planning step, giving cruise request {cruiseRequest} units/s before slowing and acceleration limits. The engine pulls the anchor towards the mean and caps their distance at {lagLimit}; that distance is now {anchorLag}. This does not bound every member’s slot error.

step4.title: Measure shape and arrival separately
step4.text: The largest member-to-slot gap is {slotError}, compared with the chosen allowance {budget}. Arrival is a separate study-local test: distance to the final slot at the beacon must be at most {arrivalDistance}, and speed at most {arrivalSpeed}. slotError = maximum distance(member, engine.slotPosition(formation, assigned slot))
for each member:

intuition.text: The harbour launcher can predict where a shot lands without firing it. Treat its signed miss as feedback: a short prediction and a long prediction surround a useful angle, and each new prediction narrows that choice. The important result is an angle with a measured small miss, rather than an attractive-looking arc.
intuition.situation: A training launcher must hit a stationary drum while its game’s drag rule changes the flight. Reusing that flight rule inside the aiming search keeps the prediction consistent with the toy physics.

example.name: The harbour launcher finding the drum
example.description: The drum is {targetX} m along level ground. Every candidate leaves the harbour launcher at {launchSpeed} m/s; only its angle changes between {lowerAngle}° and {upperAngle}°. The local simulator uses downward gravity {gravity} m/s², linear drag coefficient {drag} per second and velocity-before-position steps of {timeStep} s. Two endpoint probes precede at most {maxIterations} midpoint guesses. A completed impact within {tolerance} m is accepted; {flightSteps} physics steps bound each prediction. The drawing currently shows angle {angle}°, signed miss {error} m and search status {status}.

step0.title: Require a useful angle bracket
step0.text: Predict the endpoint shots first. Both must reach the ground. Accept an endpoint already within tolerance; otherwise their signed range errors must surround zero. A same-side pair rejects this bracket, rather than declaring the drum unreachable at every possible angle. Endpoint probes are separate from the midpoint-guess budget.

step1.title: Predict the midpoint shot
step1.text: Bisect the current angles {bracketLower}° and {bracketUpper}° to obtain {angle}°. Resolve the fixed launch speed into horizontal and vertical velocity, then repeatedly apply gravity and drag. Interpolate the first ground crossing between the surrounding samples so the miss is measured on the ground, rather than at the last airborne point.

step2.title: Measure before accepting
step2.text: Subtract the drum position from the predicted impact: {impactX} − {targetX} = {error} m. Positive means long and negative means short. Accept only when the absolute miss is at most {tolerance} m. A prediction that outlasts its physics horizon has an unknown impact, not a successful shot.

step3.title: Retain the sign change or report failure
step3.text: Compare the midpoint’s sign with the lower endpoint’s sign and discard the half without a sign change. The candidate next bracket is [{nextLower}, {nextUpper}]°. Repeat until acceptance or the budget ends. Exhausting a budget with a remaining miss reports failure even when the next guess might have succeeded.

pseudocode.ordinary:
lowFlight = simulate(lowerAngle)
highFlight = simulate(upperAngle)
if either flight has no ground impact: fail unfinished
lowError = lowFlight.range - targetX
highError = highFlight.range - targetX
if abs(lowError) <= tolerance: accept lowerAngle
if abs(highError) <= tolerance: accept upperAngle
if lowError * highError > 0: fail unbracketed

angle = (lowerAngle + upperAngle) / 2
velocity = launchSpeed * (cos(angle), sin(angle))
repeat at most flightSteps times:
  vx = vx + (-drag * vx) * dt
  vy = vy + (-gravity - drag * vy) * dt
  nextPosition = position + (vx, vy) * dt
  if nextHeight <= 0:
    fraction = height / (height - nextHeight)
    range = x + fraction * (nextX - x)
    end this prediction
  position = nextPosition

if no ground crossing: fail unfinished
error = range - targetX
if abs(error) <= tolerance: accept angle

if lowError * error > 0:
  lowerAngle = angle
  lowError = error
else:
  upperAngle = angle
repeat midpoint prediction while guesses remain
otherwise report budget exhausted

limits.item0: The search solves its own fixed-step flight model. A different integration order, drag law or collision rule in the game can turn a small predicted miss into a real miss; tightening the search tolerance cannot remove that modelling error.
limits.item1: Reducing the midpoint budget to {shortBudget} can stop with a measurable miss outside tolerance. The comparison holds the last result after stopping; it does not imply the solver continued working.
limits.item2: Endpoint signs establish a bracket only for a continuous range-error function. Terrain collisions, target switching or discontinuous flight rules can invalidate that assumption. Same-side endpoint errors do not prove there is no intermediate or higher-arc solution.
limits.item3: The drum stays still on level ground. Moving targets require impact-time prediction, and this local angle search does not choose between low and high arcs or check obstacles along an arc.
limits.item4: This study-local search and linear-drag simulator are absent from the public scene engine. The engine supplies only deterministic trigonometry here; no whole-scene projectile behaviour is claimed.

intuition.text: A take-off marker asks Finch to arrive in a particular moving state. Reaching the painted ring while standing still is no help when the canal crossing needs forward speed. The run-up prepares that speed; the marker grants the vertical jump only when position and velocity agree with its requirement.
intuition.situation: A courier follows a straight quay towards a designer-authored crossing. The marker makes the transition from ground locomotion to airborne motion inspectable and gives an explicit reason to refuse a poorly prepared jump.

example.name: Finch crossing the canal
example.description: Finch begins at {startX} m with horizontal velocity {initialVelocity} m/s and approaches the take-off ring at {markerX} m. The ring requires {requiredVelocity} m/s within {velocityTolerance} m/s and position within {positionTolerance} m. Run-up acceleration is limited to {maxAcceleration} m/s², speed to {maxSpeed} m/s and response time to {responseTime} s. An accepted launch adds vertical velocity {verticalVelocity} m/s under gravity {gravity} m/s². The equal-height receiving pad is centred at {padCentre} m, with half-width {padHalfWidth} m. The current phase is {phase}, horizontal speed {vx} m/s and height {height} m.

step0.title: Author a take-off state
step0.text: Place the ring at {markerX} m and require forward velocity {requiredVelocity} m/s. For this canal, the vertical impulse and equal platform heights imply flight duration {flightDuration} s. Place the receiving pad where that required horizontal velocity carries Finch during the flight. The marker protocol and this trajectory are study-local.

step1.title: Prepare the moving arrival
step1.text: During the straight run-up, call the scene engine’s matchVelocity with the marker’s required velocity. It requests the velocity gap divided by {responseTime} s and caps acceleration. Advance the new horizontal velocity over {timeStep} s. This is a velocity target, so the run-up keeps moving through the ring rather than slowing towards a stop.

step2.title: Check both conditions at the marker
step2.text: At the first sampled encounter with the marker window, check position error and horizontal velocity error together. Only a valid state receives the vertical launch impulse; preserve the actual horizontal velocity instead of replacing it with the requested one. A failed encounter ends this one-pass example as rejected, with no claim to simulate emergency braking.

step3.title: Follow the accepted flight
step3.text: After take-off, horizontal velocity remains constant and height follows the constant-gravity equation. Sample until the equal-height ground contact, then compare the contact position with the receiving pad. The airborne calculation uses elapsed flight time {airTime} s; the current height is {height} m and vertical velocity {vy} m/s. The study stops before landing collision response.

pseudocode.ordinary:
marker = (markerX, requiredVelocity)
flightDuration = 2 * verticalVelocity / gravity
padCentre = markerX + requiredVelocity * flightDuration
state = (startX, initialVelocity, runUp)

while x < markerX - positionTolerance and steps remain:
  acceleration = engine.matchVelocity(body, requiredVelocity, responseTime)
  velocity = clamp(velocity + acceleration * dt, -maxSpeed, maxSpeed)
  x = x + velocity * dt
if the step horizon ends before the marker: report unfinished

positionOK = abs(x - markerX) <= positionTolerance
velocityOK = abs(velocity - requiredVelocity) <= velocityTolerance
if not (positionOK and velocityOK): reject this encounter
takeoffX = x
takeoffVelocity = velocity
apply verticalVelocity as the jump impulse

for each airborne sample t through flightDuration:
  x = takeoffX + takeoffVelocity * t
  height = verticalVelocity * t - gravity * t * t / 2
  vy = verticalVelocity - gravity * t
at ground contact:
  landingError = abs(x - padCentre)
  report whether landingError <= padHalfWidth
  end before collision response

intuition.text: The archive trolley treats its remaining journey as a fresh request at every update: cover the gap within the chosen response time. Far from the charger, that request exceeds its speed cap. Nearby, the same calculation asks for less speed. The trolley adopts the requested velocity immediately, so its slowing comes from smaller requests rather than simulated braking.
intuition.situation: A trolley in an archive animation needs to approach its charging marker smoothly, while the animation can set its velocity directly.

example.name: The archive trolley approaches its charger
example.description: The trolley starts at {start} on a straight aisle and heads for a charging marker at {target}. Its speed cap is {maxSpeed} units/s, time to target {timeToTarget} s and satisfaction radius {satisfactionRadius} units. Each update advances {timeStep} s; the run contains {steps} updates. The outer circle has the derived radius {taperDistance}, where the speed cap stops binding. This executable uses a study-local velocity rule: the public scene engine has acceleration-based Arrive, but no direct-velocity kinematic arrival helper.

step0.title: Measure the signed journey left
step0.text: Subtract the trolley position from the marker position. The sign chooses the direction of travel; the magnitude is the distance used by the stop decision. At this moment the trolley is at {position}, leaving {distance} units.

step1.title: Accept a region, keeping its error
step1.text: This model includes the boundary: distance at or below {satisfactionRadius} units accepts the current place. It assigns zero velocity and leaves the trolley there. Acceptance does not place it exactly on the marker, and it can stop immediately because the model carries no momentum.

step2.title: Turn the remaining journey into velocity
step2.text: Outside the accepted region, divide the signed offset by {timeToTarget} s and clamp the result to the speed cap. No separate slowing-radius input is needed: tapering begins at maxSpeed × timeToTarget, currently {taperDistance} units from the marker. The assigned velocity now is {velocity} units/s.

step3.title: Advance with that assigned velocity
step3.text: Multiply velocity by the update duration, then add the displacement to position. This update moves {displacement} units to {nextPosition}. Where the speed cap is inactive and the stop has not been accepted, the next signed error equals the old error multiplied by 1 − dt / timeToTarget, currently {errorFactor}.

intuition.text: Moss, a gallery patrol robot, keeps walking while its facing drifts. Each update remembers the previous facing and adds a small signed turn. That memory gives the trail continuity: choosing an entirely new compass direction would make each update unrelated to the last.
intuition.situation: Use this when an idle character should roam without a destination and its movement system accepts velocity directly. It gives Moss motion to watch; it does not give the patrol a route or a guarantee of visiting every room.

example.name: Moss patrols an empty gallery
example.description: Moss starts at ({startX}, {startY}), facing {startHeading} radians, and immediately walks at {speed} units/s. Every {timeStep} s it draws a signed turn rate bounded by {maxRotation} radians/s. Seed {seed} makes the {duration}-second patrol replayable. The comparison raises only the turn-rate bound to {failureRotation} radians/s. The empty gallery has no walls or stopping rule.

step0.title: Read the current facing as velocity
step0.text: Convert the remembered angle with the public engine's deterministic cosine and sine, normalise the direction and multiply by {speed}. Moss uses this velocity immediately; there is no acceleration ramp. The green arrow is this update's displacement direction.

step1.title: Draw a small signed turn
step1.text: Take the difference of successive uniform draws. Small differences are more common than extreme ones; the sign chooses a turning direction. Multiplying by {maxRotation} gives a turn rate. The seeded generator is study-local because the engine's random helpers are not public exports.

step2.title: Move, then remember the new facing
step2.text: Move with the velocity calculated from the old facing, then add turnRate × {timeStep} to that facing. The amber arrow previews the next update's velocity. This direct kinematic update is study-local: the public engine's wander function is an acceleration-based behaviour with a forward circle, a different mechanism.

pseudocode.ordinary:
direction = normalize({ x: cosine(heading), y: sine(heading) })
velocity = direction * speed

[first, seed] = seededUniform(seed)
[second, seed] = seededUniform(seed)
sample = first - second
turnRate = sample * maxRotation

position = position + velocity * timeStep
heading = heading + turnRate * timeStep
remember(position, heading, seed)
