intuition.text: Fern needs to look like a creature the player can influence. Keeping company, leaving room, drifting about and moving away from the player are separate requests for acceleration. Giving sheep and goats different strengths for those requests creates different responses from the same controller. The design work is deciding which requests apply, whom each creature observes and what happens when the requests conflict.
intuition.situation: Kit drives the sheep Fern and Moss and the goats Flint and Pebble east through Bracken Meadow. Each species has its own profile; adjust the player response and the goats' wander weight to see how those choices change the drive. These are chosen game personalities, not measured animal traits.

example.name: The Bracken Meadow drive
example.description: Kit follows a fixed eastward path. The creatures start still: Fern and Moss form the inner pair, Flint and Pebble the outer pair. They separate from either species but cohere and match velocity only with nearby members of their own species. Player response has scale {fleeScale}; goat wandering has weight {goatWander}, against the sheep's {sheepWander}. Both profiles call the scene engine's separation, arrive, matchVelocity, wander, flee and blend functions. Profile selection, perception, the prescribed wander-angle wobble and the simultaneous fixed-step update are study-local. Distances use arbitrary field units, time uses seconds and angles use radians; the engine's fixed flee range is {fleeRadius} units.

step0.title: Sample Kit and the creature neighbourhoods
step0.text: Kit is {playerRelation} the sheep. Fern reads {neighbours} sheep neighbours, excluding herself when averaging their positions and velocities. Same-species membership affects cohesion and alignment; separation still considers goats. Each creature reads the old frame, before anyone moves.

step1.title: Select a profile without changing the algorithm
step1.text: The sheep profile uses wander weight {sheepWander} and effective flee weight {sheepFlee}; the goat profile uses {goatWander} and {goatFlee}. Effective flee weight is the species weight times fleeScale, the input changed in the comparison. The common spacing and velocity rules keep the same implementation for both profiles.

step2.title: Build the social requests
step2.text: Engine separate uses linear falloff over close creatures. Engine arrive heads towards the same-species centre with a point target and a slowing radius, while engine matchVelocity closes the gap to the neighbours' mean velocity. Empty social neighbourhoods silence cohesion and alignment. The Social row adds these weighted requests; their individual directions and values appear in the worked step.

step3.title: Add wandering and the player response
step3.text: A deterministic sine wobble sets Fern's wander angle to {angle} radians; paired creatures use opposite signs. Engine wander selects a velocity along its projected circle and corrects towards it. Engine flee points away from Kit, fading to nothing at the fixed {fleeRadius}-unit range. Fern is {gap} units away; her weighted wander and flee requests have magnitudes {wanderMagnitude} and {fleeMagnitude} units/s².

step4.title: Resolve all requests with a weighted sum
step4.text: Engine blend multiplies the social, wander and flee outputs by their selected weights, adds them and caps the result at {maxAcceleration} units/s². Fern's result has magnitude {accelerationMagnitude} units/s². No request has automatic precedence: increasing flee strengthens a contribution but does not turn the blend into a safety constraint.

step5.title: Integrate together and measure the response
step5.text: Update each velocity over {timeStep} seconds, cap speed and move with the updated velocity, then publish the whole new frame. Kit's next position comes from the same fixed path. The chart shows signed eastward centre displacements of {sheepTravel} units for sheep and {goatTravel} for goats; these measure the profiles' effects on this drive.

pseudocode.ordinary:
old = snapshot(creatures)
seconds = step * timeStep
player = (playerStartX + playerSpeed * seconds, playerY)
for each body in old:
  neighbours = other bodies of body.species strictly within neighbourRadius
  centre, meanVelocity = means of neighbours when nonempty

  profile = sheepProfile when body.species is sheep, otherwise goatProfile
  wanderWeight = profile.wanderWeight
  fleeWeight = profile.fleeWeight * fleeScale

  separation = engine.separate(body, body.index, old,
    threshold = separationThreshold, falloff = linear)
  cohesion = zero when neighbours is empty, otherwise
    engine.arrive(body, centre, slowRadius, targetRadius = 0, responseTime)
  alignment = zero when neighbours is empty, otherwise
    engine.matchVelocity(body, meanVelocity, responseTime)

  angle = wanderAmplitude * engine.sine(wanderRate * seconds) * body.wanderSign
  wandering = engine.wander(body with wanderAngle = angle,
    wanderOffset, wanderRadius, responseTime)
  fleeing = engine.flee(body, player)

  acceleration = engine.blend([
    (separationWeight, separation), (cohesionWeight, cohesion),
    (alignmentWeight, alignment), (wanderWeight, wandering),
    (fleeWeight, fleeing)
  ], maxAcceleration)

  nextVelocity = clipLength(body.velocity + acceleration * timeStep, maxSpeed)
  next[body] = body with velocity = nextVelocity,
    position = body.position + nextVelocity * timeStep,
    heading = direction(nextVelocity) when moving, otherwise body.heading
creatures = next

limits.item0: Player response currently has scale {fleeScale}. With that response switched off, all social and wander rules remain but the creatures cannot react to Kit; this can let him approach Fern much more closely. Flocking alone does not supply the interaction that a herding game promises.
limits.item1: Blending gives flee no guaranteed precedence over cohesion or wander. It also cannot produce an away direction when Kit and Fern occupy exactly the same point: engine flee returns no acceleration there. Such a contact needs a separate collision or arbitration rule.
limits.item2: Flee means away from Kit, not towards a game objective. Place Kit on the other side of the same herd and the flee contribution reverses. A controller for the player, an explicit goal or a higher-level creature state must supply the intended drive.

limits.item4: The prescribed wander wobble and fixed profiles have no memory, grazing state or concept of being safely penned. The opened herding implementation adds those decisions and world avoidance explicitly; this study stops at the steering composition that those decisions can select.

intuition.text: A stop command does not erase momentum. The loading-bay cart can receive a strong braking request while its motor removes speed much more slowly. Looking at the request and the motion together exposes the gap between a controller's intention and the body that must carry it out.
intuition.situation: A rail cart must halt before a painted safety line. Its steering controller already wants it stationary; the question is whether the available brake can make that happen within the remaining rail.

example.name: The loading-bay rail cart
example.description: The cart begins at the origin travelling at {initialSpeed} units/s, with the safety line at {stopLine} units. It asks for zero velocity over a response time of {responseTime} s. The steering request has an acceleration limit of {steeringLimit} units/s², while the motor can brake at only {motorBrake} units/s². The run advances by {timeStep} s for {duration} s. This study calls the scene engine's matchVelocity for the request; the straight-rail brake policy and fixed-step integration are study-local, because the public engine has no separate motor-control adapter.

step0.title: Ask the steering controller to stop
step0.text: The velocity goal is zero. The engine's matchVelocity divides the velocity gap by {responseTime} s, then clips the acceleration vector to the steering limit. At this moment it requests {requested} units/s². This is a request to the motor, not a replacement for the current speed.

step1.title: Apply the brake the cart actually has
step1.text: The rail cart accepts only braking between the negative motor limit and zero. Its study-local adapter applies {applied} units/s². A larger request cannot create extra brake capacity; it stays saturated until the velocity gap becomes small enough.

step2.title: Change speed before moving the body
step2.text: Applied acceleration changes speed over the fixed step. Clamp speed at zero because this brake cannot propel the cart backwards, then move using the updated speed. The safety line is only a marker: remaining clearance is {remaining} units, and there is no wall clamp to hide a crossing.

pseudocode.ordinary:
requested = engine.matchVelocity(body, zeroVelocity, responseTime)
// body.maxAcceleration is the steering limit

applied = max(-motorBrake, min(0, requested.x))

velocity = max(0, velocity + applied * timeStep)
position = position + velocity * timeStep

intuition.text: A beacon above an atrium can share its ground coordinates with a drone that is still far below it. Height must participate in the steering calculation and in the success check. The nose also needs an elevation as well as a compass direction, while rolling the wings remains a separate choice.
intuition.situation: An inspection drone approaches a maintenance beacon in open air. A ground-plane adapter can put its shadow in the right place without putting the drone at the beacon.

example.name: The atrium inspection drone
example.description: The drone starts at rest and approaches the beacon at ({targetX}, {targetY}, {targetZ}), with y meaning height and z depth. It has total speed limit {maxSpeed} units/s, acceleration limit {maxAcceleration} units/s² and fixed steps of {timeStep} s. Its nose immediately follows velocity; roll is the independent {roll}° inspection pose. The last partial step is clamped to the target, which makes this a representation study rather than a braking or aircraft simulation.

step0.title: Keep the height component in the request
step0.text: Subtract the full position from the beacon position, normalise that offset and multiply by the acceleration limit. The volume normalisation shares one acceleration budget across all axes. This step is local: the public scene engine exports planar Vec2 steering, so passing its Seek an extra height property would not create volume steering. The comparison changes only the height weight from {verticalWeight} to {flatVerticalWeight}.

step1.title: Integrate a bounded velocity in the volume
step1.text: Add acceleration multiplied by the step time, then cap the length of the complete velocity vector at {maxSpeed} units/s. Move using that capped velocity. On this straight approach, clamp the last partial step to the effective target and stop; that explicit teaching rule avoids repeated passes through the beacon and provides no physical braking guarantee.

step2.title: Specify the pose as well as the direction
step2.text: Yaw comes from velocity in x/z; pitch comes from its height component relative to horizontal speed. Retain the last direction when stopped, and keep the previous yaw for a purely vertical direction. The roll command rotates the wing about the nose without changing the flight path. Local pose construction uses the public engine’s deterministic sine and cosine, then projects the nose, wing and height connector onto the motion drawing.

pseudocode.ordinary:
effectiveTarget = beacon
effectiveTarget.y = position.y + verticalWeight * (beacon.y - position.y)
offset = effectiveTarget - position
acceleration = length3(offset) == 0 ? zero3
  : offset * maxAcceleration / length3(offset)  // local volume Seek

candidateVelocity = capLength3(velocity + acceleration * dt, maxSpeed)
nextVelocity = candidateVelocity
travel = candidateVelocity * dt
if length3(travel) >= length3(offset):
  nextPosition = effectiveTarget; nextVelocity = zero3
else:
  nextPosition = position + travel

if horizontalLength(candidateVelocity) > 0:
  yaw = atan2(candidateVelocity.z, candidateVelocity.x)
if length3(candidateVelocity) > 0:
  pitch = atan2(candidateVelocity.y, horizontalLength(candidateVelocity))
roll = rollCommand
pose = localForwardAndRolledWing(yaw, pitch, roll)
project(nextPosition, pose, groundProjection)  // drawing only

intuition.text: Give the courier a feeler ahead of its travel. A hit supplies more than a warning: the surface normal tells it which way leads back into free space. Put a temporary target along that normal and let the courier pull towards it. The ray can see a wall before the courier’s body reaches it, but detection still needs time to change motion.
intuition.situation: A courier approaches the end of a depot courtyard wall on the way to an offset delivery point. Watch its forward ray meet the wall and the temporary target turn it towards free space. Then put the delivery straight ahead: the same local rule brakes and switches targets without choosing a side.

example.name: Courier at the depot courtyard wall
example.description: The courier starts at ({startX}, {startY}) with velocity ({velocityX}, {velocityY}) units/s and radius {radius}. Its delivery point is ({goalX}, {goalY}); a vertical wall runs from ({wallX}, {wallBottom}) to ({wallX}, {wallTop}). A forward ray of length {rayLength} units constructs an avoidance target {avoidDistance} units along the hit normal. Maximum speed is {maxSpeed} units/s and acceleration {maxAcceleration} units/s². The run takes {steps} fixed steps of {timeStep} s. Segment intersection and target selection are study-local; the actual pull to either target calls engine Seek.

step0.title: Cast a finite forward ray
step0.text: Normalise the current velocity and extend it by {rayLength}; at zero speed retain the last travel heading. The local detector intersects this finite segment with the finite wall segment using cross products. Both intersection fractions must lie within the segments. It reports the actual hit point and a unit surface normal facing against the incoming ray. Parallel and collinear segments return no hit in this small detector.

step1.title: Build a target from the hit normal
step1.text: A hit replaces the delivery point with hitPoint + normal × {avoidDistance}. The offset is a centre-target distance, not an automatic guarantee about the courier’s radius. The normal arrow ends at the avoidance cross. Without a hit the selected target is the delivery point, so local avoidance has no memory of the blocked route.

step2.title: Pull with engine Seek
step2.text: The model passes the selected target to the existing engine Seek function. It returns acceleration towards that target, capped at {maxAcceleration}. When the target still lies ahead, a ray hit can initially leave the pull pointing towards the wall; once the courier passes the offset target the pull points back. Detection alone never sets the courier’s velocity to zero.

step3.title: Measure body clearance and advance
step3.text: Find the nearest point on the finite wall segment and subtract {radius} from its distance to the courier’s centre. This body clearance stays meaningful beside the wall and round either end; a negative value means overlap. Add acceleration times {timeStep} to velocity, clip speed to {maxSpeed}, then advance position. The local update applies no wall clamp or collision response.

pseudocode.ordinary:
direction = normalise(velocity) if moving else lastTravelHeading
rayEnd = position + direction * rayLength
hit = intersectFiniteSegments(position, rayEnd, wallStart, wallEnd)
// Accept only intersection fractions in [0, 1]; normal opposes the ray.

if hit exists: target = hit.point + hit.normal * avoidDistance
else: target = deliveryPoint

acceleration = sceneEngine.seek(body, target)
// Seek pulls towards the selected point; it does not command a stop.

nearestWallPoint = (wallX, clamp(position.y, wallBottom, wallTop))
bodyClearance = distance(position, nearestWallPoint) - radius
velocity = clipLength(velocity + acceleration * dt, maxSpeed)
position += velocity * dt
if moving: lastTravelHeading = normalise(velocity)

intuition.text: Mica wants to reach the loading bay, but a parked trolley demands room. Adding the two requests could let eagerness weaken braking. Give Clearance ownership of acceleration while it has something to say, then let Travel take over when it declines. Think of ordered handlers returning a result: the winner supplies the whole vector.
intuition.situation: Use this order when Mica must give personal space precedence over progress towards the loading bay. It is useful only if the urgent group becomes quiet when its condition passes.

example.name: Mica approaching a parked trolley
example.description: Mica starts at rest on an aisle with a parked trolley between the courier and the loading bay. Clearance wakes inside {separationThreshold} units and has priority {clearancePriority}: {order}. A request must exceed epsilon {epsilon} units/s² to take control. Speed is limited to {maxSpeed} units/s and acceleration to {maxAcceleration} units/s², with decisions every {timeStep} s. The inner ring marks touching centre distance {contactDistance} units. Change the priority, buffer or threshold to see which requests actually move Mica; the comparison reverses only the group order.

step0.title: Measure the trolley before moving
step0.text: Read Mica and the stationary trolley from the current frame. Engine separate measures the centre gap, currently {gap}, and produces a push away inside separationThreshold. This example chooses linear falloff: the push grows with the fraction of that distance still occupied. On the edge and outside it, the push is zero.

step1.title: Build a Clearance group that can decline
step1.text: While separation is nonzero, blend its request with a request to match zero velocity over responseTime. The weights are separationWeight and brakeWeight; engine blend sums and clips them to maxAcceleration. Clearance currently requests {clearanceAcceleration} units/s² along the aisle. When separation is zero, return zero for the whole group: braking must not keep this priority permanently active.

step2.title: Build the Travel group
step2.text: Engine arrive asks for motion towards the loading bay, using slowRadius, targetRadius and responseTime. Its desired speed fades to zero halfway inside targetRadius; its acceleration is clipped to maxAcceleration. Travel currently requests {travelAcceleration} units/s². It remains a complete candidate even when Clearance will win.

step3.title: Let the first substantial request own acceleration
step3.text: Clearance priority {clearancePriority} gives the order {order}. Call engine firstActive: a magnitude must be strictly greater than epsilon, so equality declines. At this moment {activeGroup} supplies {selectedMagnitude} units/s². The losing group contributes nothing. If both decline, firstActive returns zero; ordering the groups chooses a request rather than adding them.

step4.title: Advance and decide again
step4.text: This study uses a local fixed-step integrator: add acceleration × timeStep to velocity, clip speed, then move with the new velocity. The next decision reads the new state. Steering and integration are distinct: zero acceleration preserves momentum here. Touching is measured without a collision response, and there is no automatic rest snap.

pseudocode.ordinary:
body = current Mica state
trolley = stationary body at trolleyPosition
push = engine.separate(body, bodyIndex, [body, trolley],
  { separationThreshold, separationFalloff })

brake = engine.matchVelocity(body, zero, responseTime)
clearance = zero if length(push) == 0 else engine.blend([
  { acceleration: push, weight: separationWeight },
  { acceleration: brake, weight: brakeWeight }
], maxAcceleration)

travel = engine.arrive(body, loadingBay,
  { slowRadius, targetRadius, timeToTarget: responseTime })

groups = [clearance, travel] if clearancePriority == 1
         else [travel, clearance]
acceleration = engine.firstActive(groups, epsilon)
// First length strictly above epsilon; zero if neither qualifies.

velocity = clipLength(velocity + acceleration * timeStep, maxSpeed)
position = position + velocity * timeStep
// Read these new values on the next update.

item1.supports: An ordered behaviour list uses a strict squared-magnitude threshold, exposes the selected index and retains the last small result when none exceeds the threshold.

limits.item0: With {order}, the minimum gap is {minimumGap} units and there are {touchingSamples} sampled touching moments. limits.item1: A crowd under priority steering keeps a faint shimmer in the soldier scene, as docs/dev-reference/architecture/scene.md records. Mica changes selected group {switches} times in the chosen run. A threshold and smooth component forces do not promise a final rest.
limits.item2: Priority does not plan a detour around the trolley. Passing through it in this teaching integrator is an overlap, not a discovered route to the loading bay.
limits.item3: Separation reacts to the current gap. A small clearance distance can leave too little room to brake; a large time step can miss a useful decision or a brief overlap. This integrator measures touching without predictive collision avoidance or rigid body contact handling.

item0.why: Use weighted blending when Mica should compromise between requests within the same priority group; it also explains the sum inside Clearance.

item1.why: Read blending versus arbitration when deciding whether competing requests should share acceleration or one should own it, as Clearance does here.

item2.why: Read separation to change how the trolley’s proximity produces a push, rather than changing which group gets precedence.

item3.why: Use equilibrium fallback when a blended group goes quiet because requests cancel and a later request should move Mica out of that balance.

item4.why: Reach for a steering pipeline when Mica needs coordinated targets and constraints to negotiate the blocked route to the loading bay.

intuition.text: A flare's last visible preview point is not necessarily where it lands. First ask when its height meets the surface; then use that same time to find its horizontal position. At the top of the arc its vertical velocity vanishes, but it still travels sideways. The launch has already determined its flight; nothing is steering it towards the cross.
intuition.situation: A harbour watchkeeper wants to place a marker where a signal flare from the dock roof will meet the water, before releasing it.

example.name: The dock-roof signal flare
example.description: The flare leaves the dock roof at height {launchHeight} m with horizontal velocity {horizontalSpeed} m/s and upward velocity {verticalSpeed} m/s. Gravity is {gravity} m/s² and the selected landing height is {landingHeight} m. Samples are {timeStep} s apart, but the predicted encounter is {landingResult}. The comparison changes only the selected height to {unreachableHeight} m.

step0.title: Give the two axes one clock
step0.text: Use metres, seconds and positive height upwards. Horizontal velocity stays constant; gravity reduces vertical velocity. The scene engine has no projectile predictor, so this study evaluates the constant-gravity equations locally. The drawing reverses height only when converting it to screen coordinates.

step1.title: Solve the height encounter before the range
step1.text: Set height(t) equal to the selected height and form D. The current D is {discriminant}. A negative D means the requested height is never reached. Otherwise take the later nonnegative root: it is the descent encounter, or a touch at the apex. A negative later root means both encounters were in the past. Multiply the accepted time by horizontal velocity to locate the cross.

step2.title: Evaluate the flight at a selected time
step2.text: Use the same t in both position equations and in vertical velocity. At this moment the flare is at horizontal position {x} m and height {height} m, with vertical velocity {verticalVelocity} m/s. The height chart and the drawing read these same calculated states; the arrow shows velocity multiplied by the sample interval.

step3.title: End at the event, not at a convenient sample
step3.text: If the next preview sample would pass contact, evaluate the exact root instead and finish there. The selected surface absorbs the flare, so velocity becomes zero after contact. With no future encounter, show only the bounded free-flight preview and no landing cross. Raising the requested height above the {apexHeight} m apex must produce no landing, rather than a guessed point.

pseudocode.ordinary:
require gravity > 0
use x rightwards and height upwards
horizontalVelocity = launchHorizontalVelocity
verticalAcceleration = -gravity

D = launchVerticalVelocity² + 2 * gravity * (launchHeight - selectedHeight)
landingTime = none
if D >= 0:
  laterRoot = (launchVerticalVelocity + sqrt(D)) / gravity
  if laterRoot >= 0: landingTime = laterRoot
landingX = startX + horizontalVelocity * landingTime, when it exists

for previewTime = 0, dt, 2*dt, ... horizon:
  t = min(previewTime, landingTime), when a landing exists
  x = startX + horizontalVelocity * t
  height = launchHeight + launchVerticalVelocity*t - gravity*t²/2
  verticalVelocity = launchVerticalVelocity - gravity*t
  record the state at t

  if landingTime exists and previewTime >= landingTime:
    set height to selectedHeight and velocity to zero after contact
    end the preview at landingTime

intuition.text: Ash wants to tag Reed, who is running along the quay. Steering at Reed's current position aims behind a moving runner. Ash instead aims at a temporary mark ahead of Reed. Each update replaces that mark using the latest motion; it is a forecast that can be revised, rather than a promised meeting place.
intuition.situation: A tagger approaching a runner from the side needs a lead on steady motion. Short predictions near the runner keep the aim responsive, while a cap limits how far into an uncertain future the tagger commits.

example.name: Ash chases Reed on the quay
example.description: Ash approaches Reed’s running line from the side and predicts no more than {maxPrediction} s ahead. Reed runs steadily in the main run; the comparison brings a reversal into that forecast. The ring marks tag range, and entering it measures contact without stopping either runner. Ash observes current motion, never the reversal schedule.

step0.title: Sample the runners now
step0.text: Measure the separation between Ash and Reed, {distance} units, and Ash's actual speed, {speed} units/s. This estimate uses Ash's current speed, not the speed cap or the relative closing speed. It does not solve the interception equation.

step1.title: Choose a bounded lookahead
step1.text: If Ash is stationary, use maxPrediction to avoid dividing by zero. Otherwise use the smaller of maxPrediction and distance / speed. The selected horizon is {prediction} s here. Recomputing it lets the lead shorten as Ash closes in; timeStep still advances only one update.

step2.title: Project Reed and delegate to Seek
step2.text: Project Reed’s current velocity over the chosen horizon to put Aim {leadDistance} units ahead. The engine has no pursuit function: this study calculates that prediction locally, then calls the engine’s seek for {accelerationMagnitude} units/s² of acceleration towards the cross.

step3.title: Advance and observe again
step3.text: Update Ash's velocity with acceleration times timeStep, clip its length to maxSpeed, then move with the updated velocity. Read Reed's scripted position and current velocity at the next sample. The script drives the example only; the predictor sees no future turn. Tag range is a measurement, not an arrival or braking condition.

pseudocode.ordinary:
distance = length(reed.position - ash.position)
speed = length(ash.velocity)

if speed == 0:
  prediction = maxPrediction
else:
  prediction = min(maxPrediction, distance / speed)

predicted = reed.position + reed.velocity * prediction
acceleration = sceneEngine.seek(ash, predicted)

velocity = clipLength(ash.velocity + acceleration * timeStep,
                      ash.maxSpeed)
ash = ash with { position: ash.position + velocity * timeStep, velocity }
seconds = seconds + timeStep
reed = sampleScriptedRunner(seconds)
// Repeat; only current Reed data enters the prediction.

intuition.text: The shelf runner can be close enough to collect a parcel without standing exactly on a painted cross. Making that acceptable region explicit turns arrival into a decision the task can actually satisfy. It also makes the cost visible: a larger region permits a less precise stop.

step0.title: Measure distance before moving

intuition.text: At the Lantern Gate muster, another scout should extend the patrol's wedge without requiring a newly drawn template. Treat the layout as a calculation from member count and spacing. That calculation can accommodate everyone and still produce a group too wide for the lane: accepting a count is not evidence that the result fits its surroundings.
intuition.situation: A patrol planner needs a recognisable wedge as scouts join. A preview can regenerate the destinations and check the resulting footprint before issuing any movement orders.

example.name: The Lantern Gate muster
example.description: The Lantern Gate patrol grows from {initialCount} to {targetCount} scouts on a regular joining schedule, using spacing {spacing} units in a {laneWidth}-unit lane. The engine generates a centred wedge for each count. Dots sit on proposed target rings, with circles showing body size, while the anchor stays on the lane's centre line. The chart tracks the full transverse footprint. The comparison changes only the requested membership and checks whether either muster outgrows the lane; the preview does not simulate journeys between layouts.

step0.title: Read membership before generating geometry
step0.text: The local schedule adds a scout at the first joining sample and another after each joining interval, stopping at {targetCount} members. At {seconds} seconds there are {count}. The schedule makes changes easy to inspect; a game would usually receive membership changes from its formation manager.

step1.title: Generate and centre the wedge
step1.text: patternSlots places a tip and alternates slots down the arms, extending a row after each pair. Spacing is {spacing} units along each local axis. The engine subtracts the raw slots' mean so that the anchor stays at the mean slot centre. An incomplete row can move earlier offsets sideways as well as forwards; the worked step shows that recentring.

step2.title: Inspect the proposed positions
step2.text: Add the stationary anchor to each offset to get the proposed destinations. At this sample the largest shift of a retained slot from the preceding proposal is {retainedShift} units. This is a layout change; deciding which scout should walk where and planning that journey are separate tasks.

step3.title: Check the whole footprint against the lane
step3.text: The transverse centre span is {centreSpan} units. Include a body radius of {memberRadius} at both edges: the footprint is {width} units against a lane width of {laneWidth}. The smallest clearance to either edge is {clearance} units: {fitStatus}. Generating more slots does not make the lane wider.

pseudocode.ordinary:
joins = clamp(1 + floor((step - joinStart) / joinInterval),
              0, targetCount - initialCount)
count = initialCount + joins

// The engine alternates slots along the wedge's arms,
// then subtracts the mean of all generated offsets.
offsets = patternSlots("wedge", count, spacing)

positions = offsets.map(offset => anchor + offset)
retainedShift = max(distance(previous[i], positions[i])
                    for each retained slot i)
// Draw positions as proposals; do not integrate any movement.

centreSpan = max(positions.y) - min(positions.y)
width = centreSpan + 2 * memberRadius
upperClearance = min(positions.y) - memberRadius - upperLaneEdge
lowerClearance = lowerLaneEdge - max(positions.y) - memberRadius
clearance = min(upperClearance, lowerClearance)
report(width, clearance >= 0)

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game AI library. Its generic Seek behaviour provides an acceleration calculation for steerable owners with a target location.
item0.explanation: The calculation subtracts the owner's position from the target's, normalises the resulting vector and scales it by the active limiter's maximum linear acceleration. It sets angular acceleration to zero and returns the steering output. Target access and a replaceable limiter make this a reusable behaviour; applying that output and enforcing a speed cap belong to the caller.

step0.text: Both couriers read the same positions. Mira ignores herself and only considers Rowan when their centre distance is below {threshold} units. The current inverse-square gap is {squareGap}; the linear run's gap is {linearGap}. Exactly at the threshold there is no push.

step1.title: Choose how the push fades with distance
step1.text: With acceleration limit A, threshold R and body diameter c, linear strength is A × (R − d) / R. Inverse-square strength is min(A, A × c² × (1/d² − 1/R²)); subtracting the value at R makes it reach zero at the boundary too. The current pushes are {squareAcceleration} units/s² above and {linearAcceleration} below, so inverse-square need not mean stronger at every distance.

step2.title: Add vectors, then cap their length
step2.text: Each contribution points away from its neighbour. There is only a single neighbour here, but a crowd adds all such vectors before the final length cap. The engine supplies opposite directions even for coincident positions, using the couriers' list order. Symmetric contributions from different neighbours can still cancel.

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a reusable Java library for game AI. Its Separation behaviour shows how a steering calculation can receive neighbours through a proximity service rather than searching the whole world itself.
item0.explanation: Separation asks its Proximity object to report neighbours. Each callback computes an outward unit direction, scales it by decayCoefficient / distanceSquared with a per-neighbour acceleration cap, and accumulates the result. Coincident positions are skipped. The class offers a configurable decay coefficient and works with the library's vector abstraction; applying the returned acceleration belongs to the game's movement code.

intuition.text: At Beacon gate, putting the most versatile guard in the best-looking place first can leave a specialist with nowhere useful to stand. Reserve the scarce choices first. This protects specialists, but each reservation still ignores what it will cost the guards who choose later.
intuition.situation: The gate commander must give Ari the reserve, Bryn the shield bearer and Cleo the medic distinct posts before anyone starts walking. The assignment answers who belongs where; it does not supply their routes.

example.name: Beacon gate’s guard roster
example.description: Ari, Bryn and Cleo wait for front, flank and rear posts, in that input order. Ari’s selected flank cost is {flankCost}; the resulting order is {order}, and {rosterOutcome}. Costs describe suitability independently of distance. Each moment reveals another reservation; its time is a presentation interval.

step0.title: Read a cost for every guard and post
step0.text: The column order is front | flank | rear. The complete table is {costTable}. A smaller cost means a better role fit. Neither the straight link length nor proximity to a post enters this table.

step1.title: Protect the guards with few choices
step1.text: Count entries strictly below {acceptableBelow} across the original table, before taking any slot: {counts}. The engine’s order is {order}. Equal counts preserve input order. This ranking is calculated once, rather than recalculated after every reservation.

step2.title: Reserve the cheapest post still free
step2.text: For the displayed decision the available costs are {choices}; {decision}. Every reservation removes that post from later choices. Equal costs favour the earlier column. Costs above the ranking cut-off remain eligible: the cut-off changes priority, not permission.

step3.title: Keep the links and audit the total
step3.text: After {stage} decisions: {assignments}; accumulated cost {total}. This example’s minimum complete cost is {optimum}, found by checking all complete assignments separately. The engine supplies the greedy links; that audit is a study-local diagnostic, not a replacement allocator.

pseudocode.ordinary:
units = [Ari, Bryn, Cleo]
roles = [front, flank, rear]
cost[unit, role] = read the complete suitability table

// The engine’s ranking pass:
acceptable[unit] = count roles with cost[unit, role] < acceptableBelow
order = sort units by (acceptable count, original input index)

// The engine’s reservation pass:
assignment = empty
free = all slot indices in column order
for unit in order:
  slot = cheapest free slot for unit, earlier column breaking a tie
  if no free slot: continue
  append (unit, slot, cost[unit, role[slot]]) to assignment
  remove slot from free

// The model gets these decisions from engine.assignSlots(units, roles, cost).
reveal assignment prefixes as links, without moving guards
total = sum the costs of the revealed links
audit = minimum total over all complete assignments // diagnostic only

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game AI library. Its formation package provides a configurable allocator for members whose suitability differs between slots.
item0.explanation: It asks a SlotCostProvider for each member–slot cost, drops candidates at or above a configurable threshold, and sums reciprocal cost contributions into an assignment-ease score. It sorts the least easy members first, then reserves the cheapest unfilled candidate for each. It throws when no candidate remains. Its exclusion threshold controls which slots can be considered, and its graded ranking reflects the costs of the available candidates.

intuition.text: Mara has a destination, a velocity and a limited ability to change that velocity. A steering behaviour answers a small question about that state: should she accelerate towards the depot, or reduce speed so she can finish there? Keeping that question separate from the movement loop lets us inspect and replace the answer without rewriting how Mara moves.
intuition.situation: Use this separation when a courier needs different movement goals at different times. Seek can keep her heading towards the depot; Arrive is the more suitable member when delivery requires her to slow down. The example chooses a member explicitly. Combining several simultaneous requests is a further decision.

example.name: Mara’s depot delivery
example.description: Mara starts at x {initialPosition} with signed velocity {initialVelocity} units/s and a depot at x {target}. Her speed limit is {maxSpeed} units/s and acceleration limit {maxAcceleration} units/s². Arrive uses a slowing radius of {slowRadius}, target radius {targetRadius} and response time {responseTime} s. The drawing follows {member} for {duration} s in {timeStep} s updates, while showing both candidate requests at each current state. These are toy teaching values; the actual engine functions calculate the requests and a study-local loop applies them.

step0.title: Read one current state
step0.text: Take Mara’s position and velocity before this update, together with her speed and acceleration limits. Both candidate behaviours read this same snapshot and the same fixed depot; neither moves her while calculating its answer.

step1.title: Ask each small movement question
step1.text: Engine Seek requests full acceleration towards the depot. Engine Arrive instead chooses a desired velocity that decreases inside the slowing radius, then limits the acceleration needed to close the velocity gap over {responseTime} s. At this moment the requests are {seekAcceleration} and {arriveAcceleration} units/s². Both use the same output convention.

step2.title: Choose the request the goal needs
step2.text: The arrivalEnabled input selects {member}, so the applied acceleration is {acceleration} units/s². The unselected candidate remains visible for comparison. Selecting a member is an explicit policy here; a common interface alone does not decide which request should win or how requests should combine.

step3.title: Apply the output once
step3.text: Multiply the selected acceleration by the update interval to change velocity, enforce the speed limit, then use that updated velocity to move Mara. Repeating this local loop makes changing requests into a trajectory. Acceleration is not a position command and does not remove existing momentum.

pseudocode.ordinary:
body = snapshot(position, velocity, maxSpeed, maxAcceleration)
depot = (target, 0)

seekRequest = engine.seek(body, depot)
arriveRequest = engine.arrive(body, depot,
  { slowRadius, targetRadius, timeToTarget: responseTime })

acceleration = arrivalEnabled == 1 ? arriveRequest : seekRequest
// Inspect the unselected request, but do not add it.

velocity = clipLength(velocity + acceleration * timeStep, maxSpeed)
position = position + velocity * timeStep

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a public Java game-AI library with a family of steering classes behind a common base class. That base makes the contract between a movement question and its acceleration output concrete.
item0.explanation: SteeringBehavior holds an owner and an optional limiter. calculateSteering delegates to a subclass when enabled and zeroes the caller’s output when disabled. The Seek subclass fills the linear channel with a normalised target direction scaled to the allowed acceleration and explicitly clears the angular channel. This separates calculating a request from the game’s code that applies it.

intuition.text: Nori’s inspection tug already has motion when a steering request arrives. The request says how that motion should change, so the tug’s controller must keep it separate from the velocity and turning rate it already has. Packaging linear and angular acceleration together lets one update carry both instructions without confusing either with a new position or heading.
intuition.situation: Use a steering output at the boundary between a rule that requests movement and a controller that advances a body. Nori’s pulse makes this boundary visible: the controller consumes the request, then continues moving after the request becomes zero.

example.name: Nori’s inspection pulse
example.description: Nori launches at ({initialX}, {initialY}) with velocity ({initialVelocityX}, {initialVelocityY}) units/s, heading {initialHeading} rad and turning rate {initialRotation} rad/s. For {pulseSeconds} s it receives world-coordinate linear acceleration ({linearAccelerationX}, {linearAccelerationY}) units/s² and angular acceleration {angularAcceleration} rad/s²; later updates receive zero in both channels. Each update lasts {timeStep} s and the run lasts {duration} s. This is a study-local output record and consumer: the engine provides vector arithmetic, but no combined linear/angular output type or angular integrator.

step0.title: Package the current request
step0.text: At this update the pulse supplies linear {linearOutput} units/s² and angular {angularOutput} rad/s². The linear vector uses world axes; the angular scalar changes the rate of facing. After the pulse the complete request is zeroed, so a previous command cannot remain accidentally active.

step1.title: Change linear velocity
step1.text: Multiply linear acceleration by {timeStep} s and add the resulting velocity change, {velocityChange} units/s, to Nori’s existing velocity. Assigning acceleration directly to velocity would mix quantities with different units and lose the motion already present.

step2.title: Change angular velocity
step2.text: Multiply angular acceleration by the same update interval and add it to the existing turning rate. A positive angular output increases that rate; zero preserves it. Neither value is a heading assignment.

step3.title: Advance using the updated rates
step3.text: Move with the new linear velocity and turn with the new angular velocity. This local consumer chooses rates first, then positions and heading. It has no drag, speed cap or automatic coupling between facing and the world-coordinate linear channel.

limits.item0: Zero output is not a stop command. At {coastSeconds} s the pulse has ended, yet Nori retains velocity {coastVelocity} units/s and turning rate {coastRotation} rad/s. Stopping requires a braking request or a separate controller rule.
limits.item1: Turning alone does not bend a world-coordinate velocity in this consumer. Changing only the world-y pulse from {linearAccelerationY} to {comparisonLinearAccelerationY} units/s² changes final y from {finalY} to {comparisonFinalY} units while both facings remain identical. A craft constrained to move along its heading needs a different actuator model.
limits.item2: The record’s shape does not enforce acceleration bounds, coordinate conventions or how a real body can move. The producer and consumer must agree on units, axes and which limits they enforce.
limits.item3: The rates-first update is a numerical choice. A larger time step changes the positions and headings reached during the pulse even when the final velocities agree. Outputs are sampled at update boundaries, so a pulse ending between samples remains active until the next sample.

intuition.text: The courier still wants the delivery desk when a pallet blocks its way. What changes is the next place it should head for. A steering pipeline lets the parts responsible for intent, route detail, clearance and movement negotiate that intermediate goal. The useful result is a checked movement proposal with a reason for its detour.
intuition.situation: A warehouse courier must take a parcel from the entrance to the delivery desk beyond a pallet. Its delivery request should survive a change of waypoint, while its clearance check must be able to refuse movement.

example.name: The courier, the pallet and the delivery desk
example.description: The courier carries a parcel from the entrance to a delivery desk initially {initialGoalDistance} units away, beyond a pallet. The pallet radius {palletRadius}, courier radius {courierRadius} and safety margin {safetyMargin} give a forbidden centre radius of {exclusionRadius}. The supplied upper bypass places its entry and exit corners {offset} units to either side and above the pallet, including {detourPadding} units of padding. The selected budget is {maxChecks} candidate checks per update; the comparison changes only that budget to {comparisonChecks}. The courier can travel at {maxSpeed} units/s and accelerate at {maxAcceleration} units/s². Arrive uses slow radius {slowRadius}, target radius {targetRadius} and response time {responseTime} s, and a corner is released only when the courier is close and slower than {cornerSpeed} units/s. Updates advance {timeStep} s for {steps} steps.

step0.title: Targeter: retain the delivery request
step0.text: The targeter keeps the delivery desk as the final goal while the courier negotiates intermediate stops. The grey line shows that continuing intent. This example needs only a position channel; there is no competing orientation or velocity request to merge.

step1.title: Decomposer: select the next piece of the route
step1.text: The initial route contains just delivery. After repair it contains the bypass corners and delivery. Select the earliest remaining waypoint, currently the {waypointName}. Remove a corner only when its distance is within {targetRadius} and the courier is moving at most {cornerSpeed} units/s. This deliberately makes the courier slow at corners instead of cutting across the pallet. Retain an accepted route between updates, so the bypass does not change sides every frame.

step2.title: Constraint: preview, reject, repair and check again
step2.text: Ask the actuator to preview its actual next movement towards the waypoint. The constraint checks the entire remaining polyline and that next movement segment against the inflated pallet. For a segment a→b, project the pallet centre onto the segment, clamp the projection to its endpoints, and subtract {exclusionRadius} from the closest distance. A negative result refuses the proposal. Suggest the upper bypass with offset {offset}, select its next waypoint and preview again. Each check consumes budget, including the check of a repair. At this moment there are {checks} checks and {rejections} refusals; the last route clearance is {routeClearance} and the predicted movement clearance is {sweptClearance}.

step3.title: Actuator: commit checked motion or brake
step3.text: This study supplies local target selection, decomposition and constraint negotiation because the scene engine has no pipeline. Its actuator calls the engine's Arrive function: outside the slow radius request maximum speed; inside, reduce speed towards rest at half the target radius, then cap acceleration while closing the velocity gap over the response time. Commit the same velocity-first update that was previewed. The current acceleration magnitude is {accelerationMagnitude} units/s²; the next speed is {nextSpeed} units/s. On budget exhaustion, discard unverified repairs and use the engine's velocity matching to brake towards rest. A failed update retains only its previously accepted route.

pseudocode.ordinary:
goal = targeter.position(goalX, goalY)
body = state.kinematics

route = dropReachedCorners(state.route, targetRadius, cornerSpeed)
// The initial route is [goal].
// Keep each corner until both distance and speed are small.

inflatedRadius = palletRadius + courierRadius + safetyMargin
accepted = false
repeat at most maxChecks:
  waypoint = first(route)
  acceleration = engine.arrive(body, waypoint,
                              slowRadius, targetRadius, responseTime)
  preview = integrateVelocityThenPosition(state, acceleration, route)
  routeGap = minimumSegmentClearance([state.position, ...route])
  sweptGap = segmentClearance(state.position, preview.position)
  if routeGap >= 0 and sweptGap >= 0:
    accepted = true
    break
  route = upperBypass(goal, inflatedRadius + detourPadding)
  route = dropReachedCorners(route, targetRadius, cornerSpeed)

if accepted:
  return preview
acceleration = engine.matchVelocity(body, zeroVelocity, responseTime)
return integrateVelocityThenPosition(state, acceleration, state.route)
// vNext = clipLength(v + acceleration * timeStep, maxSpeed)
// pNext = p + vNext * timeStep; discard unverified repairs.

item0.relevance: aicore is the historical companion code for an earlier edition of Artificial Intelligence for Games. Its maintainer labels it obsolete. It is useful here as a concrete implementation of pipeline interfaces and repair control flow, rather than as current engine guidance.
item0.explanation: SteeringPipe merges compatible goal channels, runs decomposers, asks its actuator for a path and selects the constraint reporting the earliest violation. A suggestion replaces the goal and triggers another pass; exhausting constraintSteps invokes a configured fallback. AvoidSpheresConstraint projects a straight direction against sphere exclusion zones and suggests an avoidance position. BasicActuator delegates accepted positional movement to Seek. The interfaces allow specialised path objects and constraints that understand them; these basic components do not implement a general path planner.

limits.item0: With a check budget of {failureChecks}, the courier stalls at the resting start. The direct route uses the available budget, so the bypass is suggested but never validated. Discarding unverified suggestions makes the next update repeat the same refusal. A safe refusal does not guarantee eventual delivery.
limits.item1: More iterations cannot rescue an impossible destination. If the desk is placed inside the pallet's forbidden region, the proposed bypass still ends inside that region, so every check refuses it. The targeter needs a reachable goal.
limits.item2: Braking is a fallback, not an emergency collision barrier. A courier moving quickly near the forbidden boundary can enter it before stopping, even when the pipeline refuses every proposal. A production constraint needs to check a safe stopping horizon.
limits.item3: The upper bypass is supplied warehouse knowledge for this pallet. It does not discover other passages, test other obstacles or model a vehicle with a minimum turning radius. The courier slows almost to rest at each corner; a vehicle that must keep moving needs a different actuator and route representation.

intuition.text: Pointing directly at the beacon leaves gravity out of the decision. The launcher must spend some of its fixed speed lifting the projectile, leaving less speed for sideways travel. Two different allocations can meet the same beacon: a shallow, quick flight and a taller, slower one. Some requests have no allocation that works; keeping the launcher silent is then a valid result.
intuition.situation: A harbour signal launcher must reach a stationary beacon on a breakwater with a fixed muzzle speed. Its controller needs a launch velocity and a clear refusal when the beacon is beyond reach.

example.name: The harbour launcher and breakwater beacon
example.description: The launcher starts at height {launchHeight} m and aims at a beacon at horizontal position {targetX} m and height {targetHeight} m. Launch speed stays {launchSpeed} m/s and gravity is {gravity} m/s². This request has {solutionCount} direction(s): the low launch velocity is {lowVelocity} m/s and the high velocity is {highVelocity} m/s. Their target times are {lowTime} s and {highTime} s. The comparison changes only target x to {unreachableTargetX} m.

step0.title: Express the beacon relative to the muzzle
step0.text: Find horizontal distance d and height difference h from the launcher. The example admits a beacon ahead of the muzzle and at or above the water. With launch speed fixed, direction is the remaining choice. The scene engine has no firing solver; the calculation here is study-local.

step1.title: Check whether a direction can exist
step1.text: Substituting the horizontal flight time into the vertical equation gives a quadratic in launch slope. Its discriminant is D = speed⁴ − gravity × (gravity × d² + 2 × h × speed²). Here D is {discriminant}. A negative result returns no shot before any square root is taken. At zero the two candidate slopes coincide and count as one direction.

step2.title: Turn the two slopes into fixed-speed velocities
step2.text: Use the minus root for the low slope and the plus root for the high slope. Divide launch speed by √(1 + slope²) for horizontal velocity, then multiply that velocity by the slope for upward velocity. Both vectors retain the requested speed; increasing vertical allocation necessarily reduces horizontal allocation.

step3.title: Choose the shorter flight and inspect both predictions
step3.text: Target time is d / horizontalVelocity. The low candidate arrives sooner and is selected here; the high candidate remains visible as an alternative. At {time} s their positions are {lowPosition} and {highPosition}. They are predictions of separate possible launches, not a command to fire twice. Each uses the same constant-gravity position equations, with no steering after launch.

step4.title: Keep contact separate from the preview clock
step4.text: Solve each candidate's water-contact time from its vertical quadratic, include that exact event, and hold its dot at the landing point thereafter. The beacon in this example sits at water height, so arriving there and landing coincide. A raised beacon would be a point passed during flight, not a reason to stop a projectile in mid-air.

pseudocode.ordinary:
d = targetX - startX
h = targetHeight - launchHeight
require d > 0, targetHeight >= waterHeight, speed > 0, gravity > 0

D = speed⁴ - gravity * (gravity*d² + 2*h*speed²)
if D < 0: return no launch
root = sqrt(D)

slopes = unique([(speed² - root)/(gravity*d),
                 (speed² + root)/(gravity*d)])
for slope in slopes:
  vx = speed / sqrt(1 + slope²)
  vy = slope * vx
  targetTime = d / vx
  retain { vx, vy, targetTime }

choose the candidate with the shorter targetTime
for each candidate and each preview time t:
  x = startX + vx*t
  height = launchHeight + vy*t - gravity*t²/2
  verticalVelocity = vy - gravity*t

waterTime = (vy + sqrt(vy² + 2*gravity*launchHeight)) / gravity
include the exact waterTime event between regular samples
for t >= waterTime: hold the dot at its water landing point
never label a time-limited preview endpoint as contact

item0.relevance: Forrest Smith's C# library supplies launch velocities for ballistic projectiles in Unity. Its stationary-target overload solves the fixed-speed aiming problem in three dimensions.
item0.explanation: The solver separates the target offset into horizontal ground distance and vertical difference. It returns zero solutions when the discriminant is negative, uses the two roots to form low and high angles, and builds velocity vectors along the horizontal target direction plus up. Equal angles yield one solution. The same file also contains a separate overload for targets with constant linear velocity.

limits.item0: The moved beacon has a negative discriminant at the configured speed. The comparison leaves its request unserved and draws no invented projectile flight. More aiming precision cannot make this request reachable.
limits.item1: A valid ballistic solution need not be a safe route. The chosen low arc can hit a wall, while the high arc can meet an overhead obstacle. Both need collision checks in a game world.
limits.item2: The beacon is stationary. Motion during the longer flight can invalidate a high arc that was correct at launch; a moving-target solver must predict the encounter rather than aim at an old position.
limits.item3: The calculation assumes constant gravity, no drag and an instantaneous choice of muzzle direction. It does not include turret turn limits, wind, projectile size or an intervening collision. This example accepts only targets ahead of the launcher and at or above the water.

item0.why: Use Projectile trajectory when the launch velocity is already known and the question is where or when the projectile lands. It is the forward prediction used to check these candidate launches.

item1.why: Use Two-arc ambiguity when both candidates are valid and clearance, flight time or tactical purpose must decide between them.

item2.why: Use Iterative targeting when the encounter prediction and aim must be refined together instead of solving once for a stationary beacon.

intuition.text: A courier can climb to a concourse without leaning its whole movement model uphill. Keep the height needed to place its feet in the level, while describing its facing with a compass direction. The route’s elevation and the character’s orientation answer different questions.
intuition.situation: An upright courier crosses a ramp to a raised concourse. Its feet gain height, but its body has no need to pitch or roll with the ramp.

example.name: The raised-concourse courier
example.description: The courier follows a straight plan route to ({targetX}, {targetZ}) in x/z, with a speed limit of {maxSpeed} units/s and acceleration limit of {maxAcceleration} units/s². A surface starts rising at x = {rampStart}, gains {rise} units over a run of {rampRun} units and supplies height after each {timeStep} s plan step. The profile and plan show the same courier. Its facing has yaw only; the final partial plan step is clamped and stopped for this teaching example.

step0.title: Steer in the ground plane
step0.text: Map world x/z into the public scene engine’s Vec2 coordinates and call Seek. Height is still stored, but it is not an input to that planar steering rule. A {maxAcceleration} units/s² budget is shared across the plan direction rather than applied independently to both axes.

step1.title: Move the plan position
step1.text: Use the engine’s vector operations to add acceleration over {timeStep} s and cap plan speed at {maxSpeed} units/s. Move using that velocity. A local final-step clamp ends this straight route exactly at the target; it is not a gradual Arrive behaviour.

step2.title: Resolve height from the surface
step2.text: The local sampler assigns height from the updated x position: below the ramp, up its linear rise, or on the concourse. The current foot height is {height}; its observed vertical rate is {verticalSpeed} units/s. The sampler is deliberately separate from steering and proves neither ground contact nor traversability.

step3.title: Keep facing upright
step3.text: Derive yaw from the plan velocity and retain it when stopped. Pitch and roll stay at {pitch}° and {roll}° even as height changes. The model therefore has a spatial position without needing a free aircraft pose. An upright line in the profile makes that restriction visible.

pseudocode.ordinary:
plan = Vec2(position.x, position.z)
planTarget = Vec2(targetX, targetZ)
acceleration = engine.seek(planBody, planTarget)

candidateVelocity = engine.clipLength(velocity + acceleration * dt, maxSpeed)
travel = candidateVelocity * dt
if length(travel) >= distance(plan, planTarget):
  plan = planTarget; velocity = zero2  // local final-step clamp
else:
  plan += travel; velocity = candidateVelocity

nextHeight = localSurfaceHeight(plan.x, rampStart, rampRun, rise)
verticalSpeed = (nextHeight - position.height) / dt
position = (plan.x, nextHeight, plan.y)

if length(candidateVelocity) > 0:
  yaw = atan2(candidateVelocity.y, candidateVelocity.x)
pitch = 0; roll = 0
drawPlanAndUprightProfile(position, yaw)

intuition.text: The harbour escort has a destination and a shape to preserve. Give the route to an invisible anchor, and give each robot a place around it. The important feedback goes upwards: if the real robots fall behind, advancing their target positions faster only increases their unfinished work. Holding the anchor near their measured centre makes the plan wait for execution.
intuition.situation: Lantern, port and starboard are rescue robots crossing an open quay towards the harbour beacon. The anchor can request a pace beyond their motors. They need a common direction without being asked to chase a wedge that keeps escaping.

example.name: The harbour beacon escort
example.description: The robots start at rest in a wedge of spacing {spacing}. Each motor is limited to {memberSpeed} units/s, while the anchor can request {maximumRequestedSpeed} units/s. A {lagLimit}-unit limit holds the anchor near their actual mean; try a looser limit to see the slots draw farther away.

step0.title: Give the robots stable places
step0.text: The engine's patternSlots centres the {memberCount}-member {pattern} around its anchor, using spacing {spacing}. assignSlots gives each escort a distinct slot; all role costs are equal here, so input order resolves the ties. Keep that assignment for the whole crossing. The links join each real robot to its assigned ring; the worked step gives their positions.

step1.title: Let the members do real work
step1.text: Each robot reads its slot from the previous formation, with a speed limit of {memberSpeed} units/s and acceleration limit of {memberAcceleration} units/s². The engine's arrive chooses acceleration, reducing desired speed inside {slowRadius} units and closing the velocity gap over {responseTime} s. The study integrates velocity before position with {timeStep} s steps. Only after all robots move do we measure their new mean for the anchor. No robot teleports when the anchor advances.

step2.title: Steer the plan towards the beacon
step2.text: Inside advanceFormation the anchor requests a velocity towards the objective. It requests up to {maximumRequestedSpeed} units/s from {anchorSpeed} units per {planningStepSeconds} s planning step; its speed request fades between the {anchorSlowRadius}-unit slowing radius and the {anchorStopRadius}-unit stopping radius. The change of planning velocity is limited by {anchorAcceleration} units/s². Multiplying the updated velocity by the study step gives the muted proposal ahead of the anchor.

step3.title: Make the plan answer to the members
step3.text: The same engine call pulls the proposal towards the updated member mean by the fraction {anchorPull}, then clips any remaining gap to {lagLimit}. The resulting anchor defines the following update's slots. Clipping its position leaves its stored planning velocity intact: {planningSpeed} units/s describes an internal request, not necessarily the anchor's displacement divided by time. The chart measures actual anchor lag {lag} and mean slot error {slotError}. In this straight, equally paced wedge those distances coincide; that equality is a property of this example.

pseudocode.ordinary:
slots = patternSlots(pattern, memberCount, spacing)
assignment = assignSlots(escorts, equalRoles, equalCosts)
formation = centredFormation(slots, assignment, origin)

for each member, reading the previous formation:
  target = slotPosition(formation, assignedSlot(member))
  a = arrive(member, target, slowRadius, targetRadius, responseTime)
  velocity = clipLength(member.velocity + a * dt, memberSpeed)
  position = member.position + velocity * dt
nextMembers = all updated members

# These planning lines run inside engine advanceFormation.
gap = distance(objective, anchor)
speed = anchorSpeed / planningStepSeconds
speed *= clamp((gap - anchorStopRadius) /
               (anchorSlowRadius - anchorStopRadius), 0, 1)
desired = normalise(objective - anchor) * speed
anchorVelocity += clipLength(desired - anchorVelocity, anchorAcceleration * dt)
proposed = anchor + anchorVelocity * dt

# These moderation lines are in the same engine call.
mean = centroid(nextMembers.positions)
pulled = proposed + (mean - proposed) * anchorPull
anchor = mean + clipLength(pulled - mean, lagLimit)
# advanceFormation also updates heading from planning velocity.
commit(nextMembers, nextFormation)
measure distance(anchor, mean) and mean distance(member, assignedSlot)

visual.textEquivalent: The robots are {slotError} units short of their slot rings on average; the anchor leads their mean by {lag} units. Pulling the anchor towards that mean and capping the gap at {lagLimit} units keeps the plan near the robots.

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game AI library. Its Formation class coordinates an anchor, a geometry pattern, member targets and an optional motion moderator, providing a reusable home for formation control.
item0.explanation: updateSlots asks the pattern for each assigned slot, rotates its position by the anchor orientation, adds the anchor and drift translation, and writes the member's target. It then invokes updateAnchorPoint when a moderator is installed. FormationMotionModerator supplies the extension point for holding an anchor back; its base class averages occupied slot locations for drift but leaves the actual anchor feedback policy abstract. A game supplies the concrete anchor feedback policy through that callback.

limits.item0: The loose-limit comparison allows the beacon plan to advance while the escorts remain far from their slots. The engine's gentle pull is still present. A large allowed lag weakens coordination even though the anchor remains mathematically bounded.
limits.item1: The circle bounds the anchor's distance to the member mean. Opposing errors can cancel in that mean, so a single stranded escort can be much farther from its assigned slot. A guarantee about the slowest member would need an additional rule.
limits.item2: Moderation can delay the crossing indefinitely when the escorts cannot progress. It does not choose another route around a blocked quay, avoid collisions or decide when to abandon the wedge.
limits.item3: The pull fraction is applied once per update. Changing the study time step changes its effect per simulated second. The study uses the engine's formation and arrive functions with local integration, and omits the full scene's separation, walls and rest handling.

item2.why: Use slot assignment when distinct capabilities or roles decide which escort belongs in each place; equal-cost input order is enough for this crossing.

intuition.text: Before tuning a steering response, decide what should become alike. Cargo skiff Sora can share a pilot launch’s pace while remaining well behind it. That is success for a velocity instruction and unfinished work for a rendezvous instruction: the selected variable determines what success means.
intuition.situation: Sora joins a pilot launch travelling down an open channel. The immediate instruction is to share the pilot’s velocity. Position is displayed so the reader can see what this instruction leaves unresolved; orientation and rotation would need their own chosen errors and responses.

example.name: Sora shares the pilot launch’s pace
example.description: Sora starts at {skiffStart} with velocity {initialVelocity} units/s. The pilot starts at {pilotStart} and maintains {pilotVelocity} units/s. Sora has acceleration limit {maxAcceleration} units/s², speed limit {maxSpeed} units/s and response time {responseTime} s; the motor advances every {timeStep} s. The selected correction direction is {correctionDirection}.

step0.title: Select the property and its error
step0.text: Read velocity from both boats. Pilot velocity minus Sora velocity gives {velocityError} units/s. The position gap is {positionGap} units, but it is not an input to this correction. Selecting position, orientation or rotation would define a different task rather than tune this one.

step1.title: Choose matching or its inverse
step1.text: Form a correction target by adding correctionDirection times the velocity error to Sora’s current velocity. The selected direction {correctionDirection} requests {correctionTarget} units/s. Reversing the direction pushes the same property apart; it does not switch from velocity to position.

step2.title: Convert the error to bounded acceleration
step2.text: Call scene-engine matchVelocity with that correction target and response time {responseTime} s. Dividing its velocity gap by the response time requests {requestedAcceleration} units/s²; the engine limits this to {acceleration} units/s². The response time sets the correction strength, and an active limit can prevent the requested change.

step3.title: Update the motor and inspect both errors
step3.text: The study-local motor adds acceleration times {timeStep} s to velocity, clips speed, and moves both boats. Without either limit clipping, the next velocity error is the current error multiplied by {errorMultiplier}. Sharing a pace does not recover the distance Sora lost while accelerating; the grey link can remain long after the velocity arrows agree.

pseudocode.ordinary:
velocityError = pilotVelocity - skiffVelocity

correctionTarget = skiffVelocity + correctionDirection * velocityError

body = bodyAt(skiffPosition, skiffVelocity, maxSpeed, maxAcceleration)
acceleration = sceneEngine.matchVelocity(body, point(correctionTarget), responseTime)

skiffVelocity = clamp(skiffVelocity + acceleration * timeStep,
                      -maxSpeed, maxSpeed)
skiffPosition = skiffPosition + skiffVelocity * timeStep
pilotPosition = pilotPosition + pilotVelocity * timeStep

limits.item0: If Sora’s real goal is to meet the pilot, velocity matching leaves that goal unfinished. Even exactly equal velocities preserve any position gap, and the distance lost during acceleration remains.
limits.item1: The reversed correction is a diagnostic inverse, not a useful rendezvous controller. It grows the velocity mismatch until the speed cap stops further velocity divergence, while the position gap keeps growing.
limits.item2: Sora cannot match a pilot pace beyond its speed limit. The steering response can keep requesting acceleration while the motor clips every update.
limits.item3: The error multiplier applies only when neither the acceleration cap nor the speed cap clips the update. The initial capped update demonstrates why response time alone is not a deadline for exact agreement.

intuition.text: Mira, a museum courier, wants to walk at the pace of a cart already rolling ahead. She watches how the cart is moving and adjusts her own velocity. Once they move alike, the distance between them stops changing. That can make a companion feel coordinated, but it does not bring someone who started behind up alongside.
intuition.situation: Use this when Mira should copy the cart's motion while another behaviour decides where she belongs relative to it.

example.name: Mira pacing the museum cart
example.description: Mira starts at rest behind the museum cart, which rolls steadily at {cartVelocity} units/s. The engine's matchVelocity chooses her acceleration using response time {responseTime} s and acceleration limit {maxAcceleration} units/s². A local fixed update changes velocity, applies her speed limit and then moves both courier and cart. Change either control to see how pace agreement depends on the correction and its limit; the comparison uses a reference response time of {shortResponseTime} s.

step0.text: At {seconds} s, the cart moves at {cartVelocity} units/s and Mira at {courierVelocity} units/s. Subtract them to get a signed velocity gap of {velocityGap} units/s. The dashed arrow is the cart's velocity drawn beside Mira, so its difference from the solid arrow is visible without confusing it with the distance to the cart.

step1.title: Turn the velocity gap into bounded acceleration
step1.text: Divide that gap by responseTime, {responseTime} s, to request {requestedAcceleration} units/s². The engine's matchVelocity caps the magnitude at {maxAcceleration} units/s², giving {acceleration} units/s² here. Response time is a controller setting; the acceleration cap can prevent the requested change from happening that quickly.

step2.title: Advance both movers
step2.text: Over timeStep, {timeStep} s, Mira's new velocity becomes {nextVelocity} units/s after her speed limit is applied. Move both courier and cart with their respective velocities. The update interval advances the simulation, while response time sets the strength of the correction.

step3.title: Measure agreement without treating it as arrival
step3.text: The cart is {positionGap} units ahead, but that link never enters the acceleration calculation. When neither cap acts, each update multiplies velocity error by {errorMultiplier}. A factor between zero and one closes the velocity gap; a negative factor reverses its sign. Matching pace still leaves the distance already lost.

pseudocode.ordinary:
targetVelocity = cart.velocity
velocityGap = targetVelocity - courier.velocity

requested = velocityGap / responseTime
# On this axis, engine.matchVelocity performs this clamp.
acceleration = clamp(requested, -maxAcceleration, maxAcceleration)

courier.velocity = clamp(courier.velocity + acceleration * timeStep,
                         -maxSpeed, maxSpeed)
courier.position += courier.velocity * timeStep
cart.position += cart.velocity * timeStep

positionGap = cart.position - courier.position
drawLink(courier.position, cart.position)
plot(courier.velocity, cart.velocity)  # observations, not steering inputs

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game AI library with steering behaviours that work on a vector interface. Its MatchVelocity class is a reusable velocity controller for a moving owner and target.
item0.explanation: The calculation subtracts the owner's linear velocity from the target's, scales by the reciprocal of timeToTarget and limits the resulting vector to the configured maximum linear acceleration. It sets angular acceleration to zero and returns the steering output. This keeps the controller independent of the code that integrates movement and allows either planar or spatial vectors.

item1.supports: The public implementation divides a linear velocity difference by timeToTarget, limits acceleration and returns zero angular acceleration.

limits.item0: Mira cannot catch the cart by copying its velocity alone. Once the velocities agree, any remaining position gap persists; matching pace does not establish a rendezvous.
limits.item1: With updates every {timeStep} s and response time {responseTime} s, the uncapped velocity-error multiplier is {errorMultiplier}. A negative multiplier reverses the error, and a magnitude greater than one amplifies it until a cap intervenes. The response-time control can expose alternating overshoot; a quicker correction is not automatically better movement.
limits.item2: If the cart exceeds Mira's speed limit, she cannot match it even with continuing acceleration. This controller also has no position-based collision response: moving the cart nearer does not change the acceleration.

item0.why: Reach for variable matching when deciding which part of the cart's state Mira should copy; matching velocity does not also match position or facing.

item1.why: Use weighted blending when Mira also needs positional attraction or separation; inspect the combined acceleration because competing terms can disturb velocity agreement.

item2.why: Reach for pursue when Mira's actual task is to intercept the moving cart rather than preserve a shared pace at the current distance.

item3.why: Read time to target when choosing a response time that works with Mira's acceleration limit and the simulation's update interval.
