intuition.text: Nia, a night guard in the museum gallery, needs to keep moving without a destination. Give her a small moving point ahead to lean towards. Keep that point's previous angle, then nudge it, so each decision grows out of the last. The forward circle turns that remembered angle into a direction she can follow with limited acceleration.
intuition.situation: Use this to give Nia a roaming motion between deliberate tasks, when she can choose her next direction locally. A task such as inspecting every exhibit needs an additional rule for where to go.

example.name: Nia roaming the museum gallery
example.description: Nia starts at rest facing along the gallery. The circle radius is {wanderRadius} units and the angle nudge scale is {turnScale} radians per update. A local update cycles the explicit tape of input pairs and carries the resulting angle forward, so every turn can be replayed. The engine's wander supplies acceleration towards the target at walking speed {walkingSpeed} units/s; the local update moves with the new velocity and makes facing follow it. The drawing moves and turns with Nia, while the worked step retains world coordinates. The comparison holds the tape fixed and uses reference radius {narrowRadius} units.

step0.title: Nudge an angle that survives the update
step0.text: Subtract the tape pair to obtain {binomial}, then multiply by turnScale, {turnScale} radians per update. Add this nudge to the carried angle {oldAngle} to get {angle} radians after wrapping. A zero difference retains the angle; it does not choose a fresh direction. The tape illustrates the memory without claiming to sample a random distribution.

step1.title: Turn that relative angle into a world target
step1.text: Project the circle centre {wanderOffset} units along Nia's current heading, then place the target on its {wanderRadius}-unit radius using the carried angle. The point is now {targetRelation}, {targetDistance} units away. The local drawing keeps Nia's heading to the right, so the spoke shows the target's angle relative to her current direction.

step2.title: Ask the engine to steer towards the circle point
step2.text: The engine takes its fixed fraction {walkingFraction} of maximum speed {maxSpeed}, giving walking speed {walkingSpeed} units/s towards the target. Divide the velocity difference by response time {responseTime} s to request acceleration of magnitude {requestedMagnitude} units/s². The engine's wander caps the magnitude at {maxAcceleration} units/s², giving {accelerationMagnitude} units/s² here.

step3.title: Move, then let the next circle follow the new heading
step3.text: Apply the acceleration over {timeStep} s, enforce the speed limit and move {stepDistance} units with the new velocity. Face that velocity and retain the wander angle for the next update. The chart compares the requested turn of {desiredTurnMagnitude} radians with the next velocity's turn of {actualTurnMagnitude} radians, both measured from the current heading.

pseudocode.ordinary:
u, v = drawPairs[step modulo length(drawPairs)]
binomial = u - v
angle = wrapToSignedTurn(previousAngle + binomial * turnScale)

centre = position + heading * wanderOffset
spoke = rotateByHeading((cos(angle), sin(angle)), heading)
target = centre + spoke * wanderRadius

desired = normalize(target - position) * maxSpeed * walkingFraction
requested = (desired - velocity) / responseTime
# engine.wander computes this geometry and capped velocity correction.
acceleration = clampLength(requested, maxAcceleration)

velocity = clampLength(velocity + acceleration * timeStep, maxSpeed)
position += velocity * timeStep
if length(velocity) > 0: heading = normalize(velocity)
previousAngle = angle

item0.relevance: gdx-ai provides reusable game AI behaviours in Java. Its Wander class keeps an internal orientation and exposes both the constructed target and circle centre for inspection.
item0.explanation: Wander uses elapsed AI time to scale a triangular random perturbation, then builds a target from the owner's orientation, forward offset and radius. With independent facing enabled it delegates angular steering to Face and accelerates along the owner's orientation. Otherwise it seeks the constructed target and returns zero angular acceleration. The timepiece must advance for the perturbation to advance. This provides a concrete implementation with both facing arrangements and a turn rate expressed per second.

item0.title: Ian Millington · AI for Games, third edition · Chapter 3 Movement · §3.3.11 Wander
item0.supports: The book covers wander in Chapter 3, section 3.3.11.

item1.title: Craig Reynolds · Wander steering behavior
item1.supports: Wander retains a direction between updates, perturbs it on a forward circle and exposes controls over the variation instead of choosing unrelated directions each frame.

item2.title: gdx-ai 1.8.2 · Wander.java
item2.supports: The implementation constructs the forward-circle target, scales a triangular perturbation with elapsed AI time, and selects between Face with forward acceleration and direct seeking.

limits.item0: Nia's target angle can keep changing while her patrol stays in a narrow strip. Compare the chosen radius {wanderRadius} units with the reference radius {narrowRadius} units: a small circle beside the {wanderOffset}-unit forward offset gives little sideways deflection. A lively angle trace does not establish useful coverage.
limits.item1: This tape provides repeatability, not a sample from which to estimate random patrol coverage. Even a genuinely random wander does not promise an exhibit visit. A route or a decision about the next exhibit must supply that purpose.
limits.item2: The nudge scale of {turnScale} radians per update is applied once per update rather than multiplied by elapsed seconds. Changing the update interval changes how often Nia receives a perturbation in real time. Setting the scale to zero leaves the target straight ahead and produces a straight patrol.
limits.item3: The circle is a steering construction, not a test for walls or other people. Nia can steer towards a point through a wall. Following velocity also gives her no independent facing controller or angular acceleration limit.

item0.why: Use kinematic wander when Nia's motion can be assigned directly and the acceleration lag shown here is unnecessary.

item1.why: Read random binomial when replacing the scripted tape with independent draws; subtraction favours small perturbations but does not itself remember a direction.

item2.why: Use Face when Nia must turn towards the wander target through an angular controller instead of letting facing follow velocity.

item3.why: Read wander circle parameters when tuning the radius and forward offset; their geometry explains why the smaller circle weakens Nia's turns.

item4.why: Use path following when Nia must inspect a planned sequence of exhibits rather than hope that roaming reaches them.

item5.why: Add obstacle and wall avoidance when the gallery's boundaries must influence Nia's motion; wander never queries that geometry.

intuition.text: Nia wants to reach a loading bay while keeping clear of a parked robot. Seek pulls towards the bay and separation pushes away from the robot. Treat those requests as vectors: their weights change how much each contributes, and their directions decide whether they reinforce, deflect or cancel one another.
intuition.situation: Use a blend when several steering requests should influence the same movement update. Nia can head towards the bay and make room for the robot in a single calculation, provided a compromise between those requests is acceptable.

example.name: Nia passing a parked robot on the way to the loading bay
example.description: Nia starts at rest and seeks a fixed loading bay while the robot stays parked. Seek has weight {seekWeight} and separation weight {separationWeight}; the robot's offset below the direct route is {robotOffset} units. The scene engine supplies seek, linear separation and blend, followed by a study-local update of velocity and position. The arrows add requests tip to tail, and the chart compares their sum with the acceleration cap. A comparison aligns the robot with the route: {alignmentResult}. This example studies linear acceleration.

step0.title: Ask both behaviours about the same position
step0.text: Seek pulls towards the bay, while separation pushes away from the robot inside {threshold} units. Their current unweighted magnitudes are {seekMagnitude} and {separationMagnitude} units/s²; both read the same position before Nia moves.

step1.title: Scale each request and add the vectors
step1.text: Weights {seekWeight} and {separationWeight} scale the requests to magnitudes {weightedSeekMagnitude} and {weightedSeparationMagnitude} units/s². The grey separation arrow starts at the amber seek arrow's tip, so its endpoint is their vector sum. Direction matters: opposing requests can cancel. The weights total {weightSum}, and the engine does not divide by that total.

step2.title: Cap the length of the completed sum
step2.text: The completed sum requests {rawMagnitude} units/s². The engine's blend caps its length at {maxAcceleration}, preserving direction, to apply {accelerationMagnitude} units/s². Clipping scales the whole sum and gives neither request a protected share.

step3.title: Move Nia while keeping the robot parked
step3.text: Add acceleration × {timeStep} s to velocity, cap speed at {maxSpeed} units/s, then update position with that velocity. Nia's current speed is {speed} units/s with {bayDistance} units left to the bay. Recalculate both requests at the next position; a zero sum preserves velocity and can leave a resting courier stuck.

item0.relevance: gdx-ai is a Java game AI library whose BlendedSteering class composes existing steering behaviours. It provides a reusable container for behaviour and weight pairs.
item0.explanation: Each calculation clears an accumulator, evaluates every listed behaviour into a reusable temporary result, then adds that result multiplied by its weight. Afterwards it limits the linear vector using the active limiter. It also carries angular acceleration in the steering result. Adding a behaviour assigns the blend's owner to it, and entries can be removed or inspected through the list API. The weights are not normalised.

item0.supports: The book covers weighted blending in Chapter 3 Movement, section 3.4.2 Weighted Blending.

item1.title: Craig Reynolds · Steering Behaviors For Autonomous Characters · Combining Behaviors
item1.supports: Weighted vector sums combine simultaneous steering requests, but conflicting components can cancel; priority selection is an alternative.

item2.title: gdx-ai 1.8.2 · BlendedSteering.java
item2.supports: The implementation calculates every listed behaviour, multiplies by its weight, accumulates without normalising the weights and limits the completed linear sum.

limits.item0: With the robot on the direct route, {alignmentResult}. Cancellation can hold Nia still with the bay ahead; a stronger pull in either direction removes that equilibrium without choosing a route around the robot.
limits.item1: A weight does not enforce clearance. At these inputs, {clearanceSummary}, with a smallest centre gap of {minimumGap} units against body diameter {diameter}. Reducing separation can allow overlap; clipping limits acceleration without enforcing a safe path.
limits.item2: Seek supplies no arrival brake. If Nia reaches the bay while moving, a zero seek output at that point does not erase her velocity; a destination that requires a stop needs speed control too.
limits.item3: Rotation needs its own output and limit. The scene engine's blend used here combines linear vectors, so this drawing and its acceleration cap make no claim about how quickly Nia can turn.

item0.why: Read blending versus arbitration when deciding whether both of Nia's requests should influence movement or one should take control.

item1.why: Use flocking when Nia should move with a group as well as keep her distance; it introduces cohesion and velocity alignment as additional requests to combine.

item2.why: Use priority steering when an active clearance request should take precedence over seeking the bay instead of being weakened or cancelled by it.

item3.why: Read equilibrium fallback when the aligned robot leaves Nia at rest and a separate escape behaviour should act only after the ordinary requests cancel.

item4.why: Use arrive in place of seek when reaching the loading bay must include slowing down and stopping.
